#4916. How to preserve wealth and access funds during a national emergency

As geopolitical and technological threats multiply, the big question is whether you can hold on to your wealth and access funds when the system fails.

Amid kinetic war, cyberattacks and the prospect of the power grid failing, governments around the world have been encouraging citizens to prepare for major disruption.

In the UK, citizens have been stocking up on tinned food and bottled water in response to the government’s Be Ready campaign.

With fighter jets streaking across the skies of the Middle East, talk of a dirty bomb attack on Washington and the world’s largest software company going offline for a day, the possibility of disaster striking close to home is starting to look more realistic.

But what do you do with your money in times like these? How can you protect your wealth, but still be able to access it when the system fails?

There are two key aspects: choosing assets that maintain value even as the world goes up in flames, and being able to access funds during an emergency.

On the first point Maximilian Kunkel, chief investment officer for ultra-high-net-worth clients at UBS Global Wealth Management, tells Magazine, “We would caution against thinking of any single asset as ‘safe’ in all circumstances.”

Instead, he says wealthy investors should focus on building a portfolio that is “resilient across different scenarios,” with enough liquidity and diversification across asset classes, currencies and geographies.

The corporation’s 2026 global family office report, representing families with an average net worth of $2.7 billion, found 64% cited major geopolitical conflict as a concern over the next 12 months. These investors are not flocking to crypto for wealth preservation however.

Hadley Stern, head of institutions at Silence Laboratories and founder of Fidelity Digital Assets, explains that financial institutions may now place Bitcoin in the same category as gold, but it does not yet enjoy the same reputation as a safe haven.

“Gold has thousands of years of history [...] Bitcoin has less than two decades. But the reasoning people use is the same: a scarce asset that isn’t anyone else’s liability,” he says.

Related: Will gold’s ‘infinite mint bug’ make Bitcoin more valuable?

He advises against using it as a reliable hedge in a crisis; “I’d be careful with the hedge story,” he says. “Bitcoin is still volatile, and in a sell-off it often trades like other risk assets.”

Cash, by contrast, is handy for emergencies “for liquidity and paying bills,” but not for “holding value over long stretches,” he says.

Michael D’Alessio, chief operating officer at digital asset trading platform Talos, tells Magazine, there are early signs that Bitcoin is beginning to behave more like gold. He said that through the volatility around the US midterm elections Bitcoin’s correlation with equities remained high. However, over the same period, its correlation with gold also rose sharply, to around 0.75 on a 30-day basis as of early August:

BTC vs gold, 30-day rolling correlation of daily returns. Source: Talos/Coin Metrics

The collapse of Mt Gox, or more recently the failure of Paraguay’s Ueno Bank show that “the asset is only as safe as the system holding it,” according to Stern.

Rather than automatically moving into Bitcoin or gold when tensions rise, risk committees are asking different questions:

“Where is the asset? Which jurisdiction is it in? Who can freeze it? What happens if a counterparty or a payment rail is down for a week?” he says. “Those used to be back-office questions. Now they come up at the board level.”

Kunkel said that concern over major geopolitical conflict is encouraging wealthy families to consider “not only asset allocation, but also where assets are held, currency exposure, liquidity and jurisdictional diversification.”

The UBS report found that 88% of family offices hold bankable assets in two or more jurisdictions, while 30% are increasing or considering increasing currency diversification.

Related: Half of UK wealth advisers say clients’ crypto is ‘invisible’ to them: CoinShares survey

Fortunately the banks and custody providers are making practical disaster preparations too.

“Regulators expect firms to plan for severe but plausible events,” Stern explains, such as a cloud outage, a cyberattack, a key vendor failing or a market closed for days, and “show they can keep their most important services running through them.”

The UK government is advising citizens to stock up on supplies. Source: Gov.uk

For custody providers, that means testing whether assets can still be moved if a signing location goes offline, and how quickly operations can recover if a data center is lost. Stern says while households might prep for an emergency by stocking a full pantry:

Similarly investors need to work out which assets you can reach quickly and which you can’t, and “keeping enough liquidity to get through a bad stretch without being forced to sell.”

Kunkel says capital preservation “does not mean eliminating volatility, but maintaining enough liquidity and diversification to withstand volatility” without becoming a forced seller.

When the balloon goes up, diversification can protect a portfolio from a market shock, but it can’t guarantee access to funds if the infrastructure supporting it fails. A safe haven isn’t just about owning the right things; it’s about being able to access them when the system stops working.

#4915. Morning Minute: Nvidia Beats, Board Says ‘No’ on Jensen

Morning Minute: Nvidia Beats, Board Says ‘No’ on Jensen

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🖥️ Nvidia Beats, Board Says ‘No’ on Jensen

Six days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago, Nvidia delivered the best quarter in its history. And told him he isn’t coming back.

Fourth-quarter guidance came in at $130 billion against the $125.3 billion Wall Street wanted, with China assumed at zero.

And the CFO raised their 2028 revenue outlook to 75% year-over-year growth.

Then board chair Harvey Jones got on the call and said it plainly. “The Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” The directors unanimously accepted his resignation, and Jones declined to answer anything about the circumstances or the independent investigation still running.

Huang had publicly offered to come back hours earlier, saying he would do it if directors believed it served shareholders and employees. Trump and Elon Musk both backed the idea. A petition passed 182,000 signatures including nearly 9,000 self-identified Nvidia employees. None of it moved the room.

Nvidia has hired Heidrick & Struggles to run the permanent search. Colette Kress stays interim CEO while remaining CFO, with Jones saying the board has “every confidence in Colette’s leadership, integrity and ability to deliver.” The board also created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, to receive reports from the company’s national security and trade compliance teams.

And after all of that—the stock rose about 3%.

A 6% revenue beat, guidance $5 billion above consensus, a new product cycle shipping, and the market gave it two percent. Shares sit roughly 35% below their October peak near $240. Nvidia perps on Hyperliquid were doing nearly a billion dollars of daily volume through the week, bouncing off $150 before settling near $162.

As for impact on the broader AI trade, Nvidia proved AI demand is not collapsing. You cannot manufacture $107.6 billion of data center revenue, and margins at 74.8% mean nobody is discounting to move product. The demand-collapse thesis died on Tuesday.

Two details do belong to the bears though. Growth is decelerating from 103% to roughly 77% once you strip the extra week out of Q4 guidance. And gross margin guides down about three points, from 74.8% to between 71% and 72%. Slowing growth plus compressing margins is how multiples come down regardless of how big the absolute numbers get.

The honest read is that the AI business is fine and the AI trade has stopped responding to it. For crypto that matters more than it should, because the correlation that dragged Bitcoin from $87,000 to the low $60s over six weeks ran through this exact trade.

Now we wait for the Fed on December 9 and insight into the 2027 rate hike cycle (or lack thereof) to determine the likely near-term fate.

#4913. 6 Best Scalp Moisturizers, Tested by Editors and Dermatologists

A dry, itchy scalp can seriously mess with your day-to-day life. Beyond the maddening urge to scratch, there's the embarrassing component: dandruff and big white flakes studding your strands. And while dermatologists say that a dry, flaking scalp may be a sign of a medical condition called seborrheic dermatitis (this requires a prescription treatment like Zoryve), the best scalp moisturizers—hydrating shampoos for dry scalp, conditioners, and serums—can help.

"I always recommend starting with a gentle, sulfate-free shampoo that cleanses without stripping the scalp of its natural oils and following that up with a hydrating conditioner," says Ross Kopelman, MD, a hair transplant surgeon at Kopelman Hair Restoration in New York City. You can then follow that up with a leave-in treatment or a scalp oil to really lock in moisture.

It's also a good idea to limit hair washing to two to three times a week. "I suggest washing your hair with lukewarm water instead of hot and avoiding excessive heat styling, which can make things worse," Kopelman says. Before adding a few scalp moisturizers to your routine, here's what you should consider before shopping.

Below, shop the six best scalp moisturizers for all hair types, tested by editors and beauty experts.

The Women's Health team is regularly testing scalp moisturizers, and we found it's hard to beat this scalp serum from The Ordinary because of the exceptional value it offers. Yes, it's well-priced, but both dermatologists and testers alike love it. "It's great because it uses hyaluronic acid to deeply hydrate without being greasy," Dr. Kopelman says. He also notes that it's suitable for all hair types, including fine, medium, and thick hair, whether straight, wavy, curly, or coily.

Since I find myself constantly scratching my scalp throughout the day, I added this scalp serum to my hair routine, and after a few days of using it, I found that my symptoms significantly improved. Plus, as an added bonus, my thick, wavy hair appeared shinier and felt softer.

Our testers also like that this The Ordinary product is a leave-in treatment, too, since that makes application quick and easy (meaning there's no need to only use it on wash day).

This drugstore pick is another very well-priced scalp moisturizer that dermatologists say really works. "It has aloe, which soothes the skin, green tea extract, which contains antioxidants, and peptides, which help make the scalp skin healthy," says Morgan Rabach, MD, a dermatologist in New York City. It also has plenty of benefits for your hair: It enhances shine, reduces frizz, adds body, and helps prevent split ends.

Like our top overall pick, this is a convenient leave-in treatment. Users like the tingly sensation from the eucalyptus leaf extract, too, telling WH it not only feels refreshing but also smells great.

Our editors can't get enough of Briogeo's hair products—from the shampoo to hair masks, we love just about everything the brand puts out. This scalp moisturizer is no exception. It's powered by antioxidant-rich rosemary oil that supports scalp circulation and healthier hair follicles, castor oil for hydration, and tea tree to fight flakes and reduce itchiness. It's also formulated with bisabolol to calm irritation from an itchy scalp.

We love that you can tailor the treatment to suit your preferences—use it as a pre-shampoo rinse (a wait time of 10 to 15 minutes) or use it as an overnight hair mask. Either way, testers found the pointed tip on the bottle very easy to use, saying it made for a much more precise application.

Living Proof makes another fantastic leave-in treatment for dry scalps. Like our top overall pick, it's hyaluronic acid-based to offer lightweight (read: won't leave hair greasy) but intense hydration. It also contains vitamin B3 to help improve overall scalp health.

The product is easy to use, thanks to a precise applicator tip. And there's no rinsing required, so you can more seamlessly integrate it into your routine. Users say it works quickly, minimizing symptoms in just a few uses and almost completely eradicating any itchiness and flakes in just about two weeks. They love the smell, too—some say it's reminiscent of the ocean.

Dr. Rabach is also a fan of Moroccanoil's Dry Scalp Treatment, namely because it contains argan oil. "It contains both vitamin E and antioxidants," she says. It also contains salicylic acid, which is a gentle exfoliator that helps lift any flakes and can prevent scalp buildup that could lead to itchiness and more flakes in the future. Geranium oil also helps soothe the scalp and addresses any lingering dryness.

Like other Moroccanoil products, users overwhelmingly rave about this scalp treatment, saying it's hydrating, soothing, and smells great. We also love that a little bit goes a long way, which helps add to the overall value of the product.

If you have fine hair and want to avoid greasy-looking strands, reach for OUAI's scalp serum. "It's lightweight and doesn't make your hair greasy because it has glycerin and hyaluronic acid for moisture delivery," says Dr. Mian. It also has ingredients like red clover flower extract to help soothe an inflamed scalp while it heals. There are hair benefits, too, thanks to peptides that promote fuller, thicker strands.

It is the most costly serum on our list, but users say it's a worthy splurge for those who want something lightweight and effective with the added benefit of a great scent.

When shopping, look for ingredients like glycerin, coconut oil, jojoba oil, or argan oil, says Kiran Mian, MD, a dermatologist at Hudson Dermatology and Laser Surgery. When you have a dry scalp, it's also very important to avoid sulfates. "Sulfates, while great at creating a lather and deep clean, can be drying for the hair and scalp," Dr. Mian says.

Some scalp moisturizers are leave-in products, while others require a wait time before rinsing. Leave-in products tend to be more convenient, since you massage in and then can get on with your routine. However, those with very fine hair may find some leave-in products too heavy. If you're concerned about a scalp serum making your hair look greasy, you may want to consider a rinse-out product, which typically has a wait time of anywhere from 3 to 10 minutes. If you do choose to use a rinse-out product, though, make sure to allot time for washing your hair that day.

To find the best scalp moisturizers to quell itchiness and banish dandruff and white flakes, the Women's Health team consulted two dermatologists and a hair transplant surgeon, plus asked our team of anonymous testers and in-house editors for feedback on the products they use and love. We then put a handful of the top-rated products to the test, evaluating them for attributes like ingredient list, ease of use, and overall efficacy.

#4909. Sanctions fears loom over Russia’s regulated crypto trading launch

Russia’s crypto trading rollout faces uncertainty as companies weigh sanctions exposure, while Moscow Exchange prepares to launch crypto trading in December.

Russia’s push to bring cryptocurrency trading under government oversight is raising concerns that greater transparency could expose market participants to international sanctions.

Some companies are reluctant to join the Bank of Russia’s public registry of crypto exchangers because they fear becoming sanctions targets, a person familiar the regulatory discussions told Cointelegraph on Wednesday.

Industry representatives repeatedly asked the central bank to keep the registry private, but the regulator refused, arguing that crypto businesses should follow the same requirements as traditional financial service providers, the source said.

The concerns come as the European Union prepares its 22nd sanctions package against Russia, which is expected to include new restrictions on crypto platforms.

Russia’s new rules allowing retail investors to buy Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and Tether’s USDt (USDT) took effect on Monday, and the central bank’s registry listed 30 authorized exchange operators as of Wednesday.

The list includes major lenders Sberbank and VTB, but registration alone does not establish whether customers can already complete transactions.

Related: KuCoin suspends services in Russia and Belarus

Alexander Nam of HSE University’s Center for Decentralized Finance and Digital Financial Assets Research said the market still faces technical and regulatory hurdles, including investor testing, order execution, settlement and custody.

“Being included in the registry does not in itself mean readiness to fully serve investors,” Nam told Cointelegraph.

Alexander Brazhnikov of the Russian Association of Cryptocurrency and Blockchain told Cointelegraph that he could not identify a registered operator offering confirmed retail access as of Monday.

Moscow Exchange (MOEX), Russia’s main securities trading venue, plans to launch crypto trading on Dec. 1, with investors accessing the market through brokers rather than directly through the exchange. Cointelegraph contacted VTB, T-Invest Lab and MOEX for further details on their respective crypto trading launch plans but had not received responses by publication time.

The European Commission reportedly plans to present its next sanctions package ahead of a Nov. 26–27 European Council summit, days before MOEX’s scheduled launch.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday that Western sanctions had backfired and strengthened Russia’s economy, speaking at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen.

Russia’s broader crypto activity has declined despite its push to establish a regulated trading market. The value of cryptocurrency transactions fell 14.7% to $284.1 billion in the year ended June 2026, according to Chainalysis. The country still accounted for roughly 44% of Eastern Europe’s crypto activity.

#4908. Healthy on the Outside: The Silent Risk Dr. Nancy Snyderman Never Saw Coming

Nancy L. Snyderman, MD, spent decades helping millions of Americans understand their health. But when it came to her own health, it was a nudge from a friend that finally pushed her to get the care she really needed.

Nancy L. Snyderman, MD, began her career caring for one patient at a time. After medical school, Nancy became a board-certified surgeon, working at academic medical centers, and she kept running into the same gap: the distance between what doctors knew and what patients actually understood about their own health. Television, she realized, could help close it. “A big part of being a doctor, for me, was putting humanity back into medicine,” she says. So she traded caring for one patient at a time for caring for all Americans.

For nearly three decades, Americans welcomed Nancy into their homes through their televisions. As a chief medical correspondent, she covered wide ranging medical topics and traveled the world extensively, reporting from many of the world’s most-troubled areas. Every day, she expertly translated complex medical news into easily digestible—and actionable—information for people across America.

“I spent my whole career being the person who talked about health to help others,” she says. “I never thought I’d be the one in need of help.”

Nancy has always been active. Even now, she hikes, travels and keeps up with her young grandchildren. But being active and feeling good doesn’t always mean you’re healthy. No one knows this better than Nancy, who had no symptoms of heart disease before her diagnosis. It started when she was still a national medical correspondent, working on a story on CT angiograms and a then-new test that provided a coronary artery calcium (CAC) score. As part of her report, Nancy had the scan done herself and her score came back at 100. “I thought, ‘Oh my gosh, this is great, I aced this test’,” she says—only to learn that acing it means a score of zero.

What is a CAC Scan?A coronary artery calcium (CAC) scan is an imaging test that measures the amount of calcified plaque built up in the heart's arteries.1 It can help doctors and patients understand cardiovascular risk—even before symptoms appear.1

At the same time, she was struggling to keep her LDL-C, or low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called “bad” cholesterol, in check. High LDL-C is one of the leading risk factors for a heart attack or stroke, but also one of the most modifiable.2 To lower her LDL-C, Nancy had been taking statins—which are a commonly prescribed class of LDL-C lowering medication—for decades. “I knew what to do, and I thought I was doing the right things,” she says. “But I was never able to really get my bad cholesterol to my doctor-recommended level.”

What finally changed everything was a conversation. After reconnecting with an old friend, who also happens to be a cardiac nurse, Nancy mentioned her CAC score and stubborn LDL-C. Her friend insisted that Nancy see a new cardiologist. After some additional testing, the results were nothing Nancy ever expected to hear: severe coronary artery disease, with significant blockages in the arteries feeding her heart.

What is LDL-C?LDL-C stands for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol—often called “bad” cholesterol. When too much of it builds up in the blood, it can settle into artery walls, narrowing them and raising the risk of a heart attack or stroke over time.2

“My diagnosis was a huge wake-up call,” she says. “I thought I was doing the right things, but even I, as a physician, needed an advocate.” She’s quick to point out why that mattered: “A lot of the risks women face with heart disease can be managed,” she adds, “but only if we understand them and speak up for ourselves.”

Nancy’s experience is far more common than many women realize. Heart disease remains the leading cause of death for women in the United States3—yet only about half (56%) of women recognize it as their number one threat.3 “One of the most dangerous things about heart disease is how quietly it can develop,” says Sirisha Vadali, MD, a board-certified cardiologist in Scottsdale, Arizona. “It can progress silently, even when you feel completely healthy,4 and women in particular may not have the obvious warning signs we’ve all been taught to watch for.”

So much of that hidden risk traces back to a single number: LDL-C. When there’s too much of this “bad” cholesterol circulating, it doesn’t just sit in the blood. It works its way into the artery walls and builds up as a sticky plaque, narrowing them and raising the risk of a heart attack or stroke over time.5,6 “It isn’t only how high your LDL-C is today,” Dr. Vadali says. “It’s how high it has been, and for how long. The longer it’s too high, the more cardiovascular risk accumulates.”⁵

For Nancy, the lesson was humbling: expertise is not immunity. “You can be the most informed person in the room and still miss a health warning in yourself,” she says. It sometimes takes a push from a loved one to take the necessary action.

After her diagnosis, Nancy did exactly what she had spent years urging her viewers to do: she partnered with her cardiologist and built a plan. Together, they assessed her individual risk factors and set a clear target for her LDL-C to help lower her cardiovascular risk.

Getting there was more challenging than Nancy realized. “Despite standard treatment, diet, and exercise, my LDL-C was still too high, and we needed to lower it to my doctor-recommended LDL-C goal,” she says.

That gap—between lower and a guideline-recommended target—is one Dr. Vadali sees constantly. “When it comes to LDL-C, lower is better, but ‘lower’ isn’t the same as reaching the guideline-recommended goal for your unique risk factors,” she says.

What are the Guideline-Recommended Goals?The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia recommends specific LDL-C goals based on individual risk. For example, below 70 mg/dL for people with diabetes and multiple cardiovascular risk factors, and below 55 mg/dL for those with cardiovascular disease at very high risk.7,*

“Knowing your LDL-C number—and talking with your doctor about what’s right for you—is one of the first steps toward understanding your risk level,” Dr. Vadali adds.

She’s also quick to retire a persistent myth. “For a lot of people, especially those already at increased cardiovascular risk, diet and exercise alone may not be enough to get LDL-C to the guideline-recommended goal,” Dr. Vadali says. “That’s not a personal failing. It’s biology. Sometimes the body needs additional help, and that’s worth a conversation with your doctor.”

For Nancy, that additional help became part of her plan. Working with her cardiologist, she started treatment with REPATHA® (evolocumab) to help lower her LDL-C and reduce her risk of a major cardiovascular event.

Repatha® is an injectable prescription medicine used:

Please see additional Important Safety Information below and full Prescribing Information.

These days, treatment is a welcome part of Nancy’s routine. “Every two weeks, I give myself an injection and have built a small ritual around it as part of my treatment plan to help keep my LDL-C at the goal my doctor recommended,” she says. “I can take it in the comfort of my own home or on the go† which is a treatment that can fit into my routine.”

Nancy is careful to say her path is her own. “I’m sharing my experience as a patient, but everyone’s situation is different,” she says. “What mattered was working with my doctor to figure out what was right for me. That’s what I want for every woman reading this to consider.”

Dr. Vadali says REPATHA is a treatment she has consistently recommended for appropriate patients. “I prescribe REPATHA because we know it starts working quickly,” she says. “For high-risk patients, keeping LDL-C lower will help reduce their risk of a life-altering event like a heart attack or stroke.”

If one thread runs through Nancy’s story, it’s the one so many women will recognize: the tendency to take care of everyone else first. “Women wear a lot of hats, and most of them involve caring for other people,” she says. “We don’t always stop to care for ourselves.”

That’s the habit she’s determined to break—in herself, and in the women who’ve heard important health messages from her for years. Her message today isn’t fear; it’s agency. “I want women to proactively understand their cardiovascular risk before something forces them to,” she says. “Ask the question: What’s my risk, and what can I do about it?”

Nancy’s ask is simple: Talk to your healthcare provider about your LDL-C and your personal cardiovascular risk factors. Get your LDL-C tested, know your doctor-recommended LDL-C goal and—if needed—make a plan with your doctor to help you reach it.

“This is the health story I never expected to tell,” Nancy says. “But if telling it means one more woman picks up the phone and calls her doctor, then it’s the most important one I’ve ever shared.”

What are the possible side effects of Repatha®?

Repatha® can cause serious side effects including serious allergic reactions. Stop taking Repatha® and call your healthcare provider or seek emergency help right away if you have any of these symptoms: trouble breathing or swallowing, raised bumps (hives), rash or itching, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, throat or arms.

The most common side effects of Repatha® include: runny nose, sore throat, symptoms of the common cold, flu or flu-like symptoms, back pain, high blood sugar levels (diabetes) and redness, pain, or bruising at the injection site.

Tell your healthcare provider if you have any side effects that bother you or that do not go away.

These are not all the possible side effects of Repatha®. Ask your healthcare provider or pharmacist for more information. Call your healthcare provider for medical advice about side effects.

#4906. The 24 Best Pieces of Hiking Gear, According to Outdoor Editors

Must-pack picks for day hikes, expedition treks, and everything in between.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE BEST HIKING season is in full swing (fall, and we’ll die on that hill). And winter hiking isn’t that far ahead. So, it’s high time to get your go-to trail gear dialed in. Check your backpack for rips, reseal your tent seams, and make sure there’s enough tread on your favorite hiking boots (or shoes).

If anything needs replacing or upgrading, we’ve put together a guide to the best hiking gear, according to continual testing by our team of outdoor editors and experts. From UPF clothing and waterproof shoes to camp stoves and portable power packs, here’s everything we always pack when hitting the trail, whether for a day hike or even looking to be out there for a few days. And for cooler treks, there’s always some cold weather hiking gear made specific for the task.

As an outdoors writer, I’ve spent countless weeks outside each year for decades. During that time, I've put the most popular hiking gear to the test in places like Utah's national parks, the White Mountains of New Hampshire, the vast deserts of Big Bend National Park, Antarctica, and beyond. I also consulted with Senior Gear and Reviews Editor Ryan Brower on his top picks, research, and some of his own personal testing. While testing hiking gear, we've been sure to take thorough notes on comfort, usefulness, weight, durability, materials, functionality, and more.

So, whether you're looking for a featherweight daypack for afternoon peak-bagging or need the perfect stove for a full-fledged expedition, we've got you covered with the best hiking gear.

The latest version of the Adidas Terrex Freehiker blends understated street-friendly style with serious trail-ready chops. The low-key aesthetic (especially in core black) plays well with just about any casual outfit, making it a great travel-friendly shoe when you want to pack just one. But, with a Continental rubber outsole and liberal use of Gore-Tex, it’s ready for whatever off-pavement adventures you’re cooking up.

Osprey’s Kestrel 45 is the perfect “all things for all hikers” pack, especially for those looking to buy just one bag. The 45-liter capacity is well-sized for day hikes and overnighters. It features a classic rucksack silhouette, but with all the best features of a modern pack, including comfortable straps and a hip belt, plus a well-ventilated back panel. Storage (pockets, loops, and lash points) is well thought out, and it’s hydration reservoir compatible to boot.

Mammut’s deceptively simple Runbold IV hiking pants are among the best we’ve ever worn. The lightweight, four-way stretch fabric and adjustable waistband are crazy comfortable and allow you to move freely on the trail. Four zippered pockets offer just enough storage for your essentials, and all keep everything close to the body thanks to a more streamlined, athletic fit than most.

It’s not quite a hiking boot, a hiking shoe, or a trail runner—it’s somehow neither and all three in one. The lightweight construction and stiff upper support fast-moving day hikes over challenging terrain. A rock-solid blend of technical materials—namely Gore-Tex Invisible Fit, Vibram Megagrip, and ballistic mesh—makes for our favorite hiking footwear of the year. It’s durable, comfortable, sticks to anything, and is completely waterproof too.

At a minimum, a smartphone and satellite messenger are required packing for most hikers these days, so it’s always good to carry backup power for both. Nestout’s 10000mAh Power Bank is compact, relatively lightweight, and waterproof, making this middle-of-the-pack model the perfect solution for most hikers. Every model in the lineup provides USB-C and/or USB-A ports for keeping your most essential gadgets humming in the backcountry.

Hardcore hikers could argue the virtues of Merino versus synthetic until the sun goes supernova. For us, a blended construction of both is best. Smartwool’s new Active Mesh Short Sleeve T takes a mostly Merino wool design and adds just the right amount of Lyocell and polyester. The result is a near-perfect hiking shirt that’s lightweight, breathable, quick wicking, and odor-resistant.

We’ll take a collapsible water bottle over a traditional Nalgene any day of the week. This 1-liter model is lightweight, inexpensive, and collapses down very small when empty. Plus, the capacity and built-in filter make this a no-brainer for using as your main water bottle or as a backup. With even a remotely drinkable water source along your route, you’re guaranteed clean, potable hydration almost indefinitely.

The right insect repellent is key for spraying on both yourself and your gear. For the latter, we treat all of our outerwear (plus boots and socks) with this purpose-built solution from Sawyer. The permethrin-based product is safe for most fabrics and creates a durable, effective layer of skin-safe protection that fends off ticks, mosquitoes, and other bitey bugs while lasting over a month, even when machine-washed.

UPF hoodies suffer from a sea of sameness. That’s why the Path Projects Wadi 2.0 stands out: It feels and performs differently. The difference being the Toray Fieldsensor Byokan fabric that Path Projects uses. It’s a lightweight material that’s just as durable while also wicking moisture incredibly well. A snap on the hood provides even better neck coverage (and keeps the hood on when moving quickly), and welded sleeve cuffs help your sleeves go over your hands or be pushed up.

True to its namesake, Darn Tough’s socks offer bulletproof durability that I haven’t found in any other sock brand. Their Hike Micro Crew is my go-to for every hike with seamless toe construction and a just-right stretch and cushioning that’s just as comfortable at mile 10 or 100. It’s designed with a “performance fit” that stays put without slipping or bunching, which translates to blissful blister-free hiking. It’s pricey compared to other brands, but I’ve had several pairs for years and they still look good as new. Plus, DT backs all of their products with an unconditional lifetime guarantee.

Even for hikers not regularly trekking out after dark, packing a headlamp just in case is wise. This basic model from Black Diamond is simple, easy to use, and budget-friendly. The compact, low-profile design practically disappears in any backpack, and it can run off of two different types of battery (either standard AAAs or BD’s own rechargeable 1500 lithium-ion cell).

Nothing beats a zip-up fleece hoodie as an extra layer for maximum “toss in the backpack” versatility, and Marmot’s PrimaLoft Evolve Aerothermal Hoody has been my go-to for months now. The inside is as soft as a teddy bear, while the 100 percent recycled ripstop polyester shell helps block some wind and light rain. As the name implies, it’s bolstered with a good dose of PrimaLoft Evolve, making it ideal as an insulating layer in cold weather and a standalone outer layer the rest of the year. At just 10 ounces, it’s incredibly lightweight and packs down small, too, meaning it’s perfect as a “just in case” layer.

Your smartphone might be the most expensive piece of gear in your hiking loadout, so why not protect it on the trail? OtterBox’s Sole Series Pack provides rugged protection via a rubberized shell and raised edges to shield your screen—all with a dash of modern style. A clever elastic rope on the back offers extra storage space for small essentials like lip balm or your driver’s license.

You can’t rely on your smartphone in the backcountry. For couples or groups hiking together, dedicated off-grid-ready communication is essential. Rocky Talkie’s Mountain Radio is ridiculously small and clips to a backpack so it stays out of the way until you need it. It’s great for regular check-ins or keeping in contact if you’re ever separated from the group, especially in cell service dead zones. Plus, the four-day battery life is ideal for longer treks.

Trekking poles are a godsend over difficult terrain. For those times when you need to prioritize featherweight, travel-friendly design over hardcore durability and heavy-duty usability, Helinox’s Passport TL115 are superb. They collapse to a pack-friendly 14 inches when not in use, but adjust to accommodate a wide variety of hikers once unfurled to their max length of 45.5 inches. With EVA foam grips, DAC aluminum alloy shafts, and a lightweight design (just 11.5 ounces for the pair), these are the perfect balance for most hikers’ needs.

Read More: Do I Need to Use Trekking Poles?

When even a daypack is a little too much, a sling is just the trick. REI’s Trailmade Hydration Sling is purpose-built for carrying just enough water and your smallest essentials for a few hours on the trail. I love that it includes a HydraPak water bottle (which makes the already reasonable price feel like a steal), but is also hydration reservoir compatible. The interior is roomy enough for up to 4.5 liters’ worth of gear (think car keys, bug spray, trail maps, and the like), and a stretchy pocket on the padded shoulder strap is the perfect place to stash your smartphone.

Packing a camp chair for a day hike or even longer backcountry excursions might seem an unnecessary luxury. But don’t knock it till you’ve tried it. Crazy Creek’s ultra-portable Hex 2.0 folds and rolls for easy transport, but sets up in seconds at camp or vistas to provide the perfect place to pseudo-lounge after a long day on the trail.

The new PreCip Evo Pro is something of a unicorn in waterproof shells. It’s lightweight, packable, and 100 percent seam-taped for maximum waterproofing—heavier duty than most featherweight “just in case” rain jackets, but lighter and more packable than the sort of hardcore shell you’d pack for a week in the PNW backcountry. Translation: It’s the perfect level of protection against rain for most hikers. Plus, it’s reasonably priced to boot.

Peak Design’s entire line of cleverly designed backpacks is endlessly versatile. The entry-level 18-liter version of the brand’s fan-favorite Outdoor Backpack is perfectly suited for fast-moving, light-packing summit assaults and quick day hikes. The design transitions seamlessly from the office (or airport or train station) to the trail with a rugged-enough construction and streamlined aesthetic that provides everything you need and nothing you don’t in a hybrid daypack.

First and foremost, you might not need any gear other than hiking shoes (or boots) and the clothes on your back. Hiking can be as simple as a 20-minute walk on a path to a multiweek expedition through the wilderness. Hiking more than 30 minutes? You probably want to figure out some sort of hydration at the least. The shorter the hike, the less gear (in theory) you should be toting with you.

Depending on how deep in the wilderness you’re going (or not going) will determine what sort of gear you might need. Even if it’s only a hike for a few hours, if you’re going into wilderness it takes a different mindset for preparedness (and gear) than it does walking on a dirt path in a park in town. The more remote your hike, the more gear you will probably end up needing.

Weather is a big factor when going on a hike. In cooler climates (or when going up in altitude) you’ll need to factor in layers for warmth. In warmer climates, water will be even more important and lighter layers that can shed moisture and protect you from the sun are key. The conditions of the trail (wet, muddy, rocky, dry, etc.) also determine your footwear choice.

The great thing about hiking is you don’t need any experience to start. The most veteran hikers can share the same trails with first-timers, and everyone in between. But knowing what you’re capable of and comfortable with is important. Hiking with a friend is always recommended, but if hiking solo, make sure you inform someone of your location and timing.

Mike Richard has traveled the world since 2008. He's kayaked in Antarctica, tracked endangered African wild dogs in South Africa, and survived a near-miss great white shark attack in Mexico. #4904. Movie2K Defendant Could Hand Over 40,000 Bitcoin to End Trial—and Stay a Billionaire

Movie2K Defendant Could Hand Over 40,000 Bitcoin to End Trial—and Stay a Billionaire

The alleged operator of defunct movie piracy site Movie2K could walk away from his trial in Germany and remain a billionaire, under a deal offered by the judge in the case.

The presiding judge at the Leipzig Regional Court has offered to drop tax evasion and money laundering charges against the 43-year-old main defendant if he hands over 40,000 BTC, public broadcaster MDR reported last week. He would also have to pay €38 million ($42 million) in compensation for potential victims, according to MDR.

Saxony's Office of the Public Prosecutor General confirmed the offer to news agency dpa, tech outlet heise reported on Tuesday. The 40,000 BTC would be worth around €2.36 billion ($2.6 billion) at current prices, according to heise.

But prosecutors believe the defendant holds a total of about 56,000 BTC. If he accepts, he could keep around 16,000 BTC, worth roughly €940 million ($1 billion) today and more than €1 billion when the offer was made.

A co-defendant has been offered a deal to hand over 600 BTC and pay €17 million ($19 million), and his lawyer said she could accept it, according to MDR. The main defendant's lawyers are considering the offer. The trial resumes on December 3 and could end before Christmas.

Movie2K offered hundreds of thousands of pirated films before shutting down in 2013. Its operators made money from advertising and subscription traps, and invested much of it in Bitcoin when it traded far below today's prices.

The copyright violations are time-barred, so the trial, which began in February, has focused on money laundering and tax evasion. The judge has reportedly expressed doubts about proving some of the charges, in part because legally and illegally acquired Bitcoin may have been mixed in the defendant's accounts, heise reported.

The main defendant was arrested abroad in 2023, and in early 2024 handed over nearly 50,000 BTC. Authorities in Saxony sold the coins later that year, raising about €2.64 billion ($2.9 billion), which is held in a state judicial treasury account. The money still belongs to the defendant until there is a final ruling, according to heise. Germany's government was left holding less than $300 million in Bitcoin after the sales.

Blockchain analytics firm Arkham said last year that German authorities had failed to seize some 45,000 BTC linked to the site.

The offer comes days after German lawmakers approved new powers allowing customs officials to seize assets, including crypto, of doubtful origin without first opening a criminal case. Under that law, owners of significant assets would have to show they were lawfully obtained.

In an exclusive interview with Women’s Health, the actor reflects on her time in the ballroom.

Dancing with the Stars fans let out a collective gasp Tuesday night. Jenna Dewan and her partner, Val Chmerkovskiy, had earned one of the night’s top scores: 28 out of 30. They also won their dance-off against Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik, tying for second on the leaderboard with Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov. Then host Alfonso Ribeiro called Dewan’s name, eliminating her from competition.

“I had a great time, and I loved getting to share that with the world,” she said, moments after being eliminated. “All love.”

Not even 48 hours later, Jenna sat down with Women’s Health to share her story.

Jenna Dewan: Overall, it’s really been the saying, “Two things can be true at once.” There's so many different emotions, and it's kind of hard to even put into words because obviously doing a show like this is such an enormous undertaking, and it's physically, emotionally, mentally, spiritually intense. And so, when that's just finished, it's like a light switch goes off, and then you almost don't even know where you are.

I feel all kinds of things. I feel mostly proud. I feel really proud of myself, and I feel proud of the last dance we gave on the ballroom floor, and I feel obviously sad that it's over, that I don't get to give any more dances out there and create any more special pieces. So I think it's really both. I feel really proud of us, and I feel fulfilled, and I feel filled up, and I also feel sad that the journey of creating dances is over.

JD: When you are going through the show, it feels like any week could be you. The show is not necessarily a show about dance. It's not necessarily a competition about the best dancer. It's not about the best dance you give. It's so many other elements that go into it, which is great on a reality show front-end. It makes people tune in for all different kinds of reasons, but in doing that, you never know how it's going to go.

Once it started whittling down, it was the two of us. You kind of come to a place of like, “Okay, this could be our moment.” And I had a feeling—it was a tough week as far as some of the online noise, I would say, that goes with doing the show. So it definitely wasn't out of my mind that it could be a possibility.

Even before Jenna stepped onto the DWTS dance floor, viewers debated whether she belonged in the competition. How much prior dance experience a celebrity contestant can have—while still being considered a fair competitor—has long been a point of debate among viewers.

Jenna started her career as a dancer, where she toured alongside legendary performers, including Janet Jackson (she appeared in two music videos of the singer’s). In 2006, she landed her breakout role in Step Up, in which she played a classically trained ballerina. She was the host for television shows World of Dance and Flirty Dancing as well as a judge on Come Dance with Me. Many fans of DWTS cited Jenna’s impressive resume as an unfair advantage. “How is Jenna Dewan part of this? She was a professional dancer. Hello! So unfair already,” one X user wrote on the platform after the official season 35 cast announcement.

It should be noted, however, Jenna is not the first celebrity to join the show with previous dance experience—and it’s safe to say she’ll be far from the last. Stars like Heather Morris, Jordan Fisher, and Charli D’Amelio have all undergone criticism for joining the show in the past, despite having a substantial leg up among fellow contestants. Even Alfonso, the show’s current host and season 19 winner, had prior dance experience.

JD: I will say, through the history of watching the show and what I know about the show, is I've seen there be an issue with people with dance backgrounds, and that obviously there's a lot of opinions on whether we should even have people compete on the show that have dance backgrounds.

I definitely asked quite a few times, “Are you sure you guys want me on the show?” But the incredible people who do the show were really confident in expressing to me that this show had changed a lot, and that it’s not Dancing with the Stars Who Have Never Danced. They wanted a very dynamic cast with all different levels and strengths they bring to the ballroom. I knew it would be an uphill battle for me for sure, just from the patterns of the show and the loyalists of the show and how they feel. But ultimately, the gift of doing something just for myself was really intoxicating, and it won over any sort of doubts or hesitations I had.

JD: The hardest part of the show, I would say, is it really teaches you that joy and difficulty can exist together. There were so many highs of this journey, and then so many moments of frustration and negative noise and criticism that is honestly sad, because it tries to suck out the joy from the experience.

Even for myself with a dance background, it is vulnerable to put yourself out there in the ballroom every Tuesday and be like, “Hey guys, watch my dance and tell me what you think.” And then you have the whole other element of this social, online, noisy world that is almost like they're looking to tear people down, and I felt that that was an unfortunate shade to this show that didn't need to happen.

JD: Part of the journey of the show is interesting because for the first good couple weeks, you rarely see any of the other contestants, because you are really in your own rehearsal space, and you're just trying to get the dances down as fast as you can with your partner. I think it was rare seeing people in the hallways and connecting with some of the contestants. But yeah, we definitely would talk.

I think at one point Connor [Wood] made me laugh so hard because he said he had seen some of the online social negativity, and he said, “Everyone needs to go back to journaling.” I laughed so hard, because he is exactly right. At some point, we all thought it was okay to just get online and to be mean for no reason. We are real human beings that see this and feel this, and I think that that gets forgotten.

When we did the team dance, that was when we really were able to start bonding as the contestants, because we were finally together working towards one dance and in a room together. I absolutely love them, and we were all definitely talking about this and sharing our experiences with this, and how most of us at that point, I think, had taken it off our phone or turned off social media.

JD: Naturally, because of my dance background, there were really high expectations that I put on myself, and that the world was putting on me. I didn't even realize it was happening, but it was creating this feeling that I needed to let go of perfection and kind of just get comfortable being seen and just being there. I didn't need to prove anything.

I think I just realized how much of my life I spent wanting to get things right. And this experience really challenged me in that way, because what I realized is, you just can't grow if you're constantly worried about being perfect. I had to learn to be a little uncomfortable, to be critiqued again, to make some mistakes, to be vulnerable, and just let people see me in the middle of figuring something out. There's actually a lot of freedom in that, because I didn't have ballroom dance down perfectly by the time I got out there.

JD: I thought that every dance we did. I thought that during the week two jive, and it was intriguing to me that [the judges] were so critical of certain dances. However, when I look back, there was a lot of growth for me.

There was a whole element of this that was sort of discovering my strength in a new way because I have had three children, I've navigated huge life transitions, I've built a career, a family, a life, And now, I'm stepping into this show where I'm pushing myself physically, emotionally, creatively in a way that I haven't in years. So I think I just surprised myself with how strong I am, and not just physically, but emotionally.

Jenna also faced an unexpected complication when her partner, Val, was suspended for one episode of the show following a social media post he made about DWTS judge Carrie Ann Inaba. After Carrie Ann criticized his wife, fellow pro dancer Jenna Johnson, for including what she considered an illegal lift in her routine with Harry Shum Jr., Val posted, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.” The now-deleted post was widely interpreted as a reference to the 2022 Academy Awards, when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock after making a joke about his wife, Jada Pinkett Smith.

Carrie Ann appeared to interpret the post as a threat. She shared a screenshot of a Page Six story about it on Instagram, writing, “So this is what we are doing now?”

On Oct. 17, DWTS production company BBC Studios said Val would not participate in the Oct. 20 episode. Jenna danced with pro Alan Bersten in his place.

JD: I said this, and I really mean this, that I did not foresee having as many challenges as I did that were thrown at me during my Dancing with the Stars journey. However, the challenges of it gave me an opportunity to walk my talk, and I always think that when that happens, you can go back to your true north, to what’s your intention for doing something. How do you want to show up as a human when you’re experiencing challenges? And I kept going back to my kids. When the mid-season suspension happened, and all these things were going on, I thought, “I have a real opportunity here. I can be annoyed and bitter and upset about this, or I can show up with grace and love and joy and focus on the moment.”

That particular week was about my mom and my dedication to her. And she was in town, thrilled to have this dance with me, and thrilled to experience this moment. And I thought that this is something she's going to remember. We're all going to remember my family forever. Let's focus on that, and let's not worry about all of this that's going on.

JD: I’ve seen that, and I feel like with just life in general, even outside of Dancing with the Stars, that is absolutely something that most females have experienced. I think there's been a great change in our world, but I think for years upon years upon years, women have had a fight against misogyny and inherent bias. Women at times in life are just held to a different standard than men, and I think that that is a real reflection.

We're expected to be exceptional, but also humble and confident, but not too confident, skilled, but not struggling enough to earn praise. There's all this pressure on women. It feels like sometimes if a woman is strong or capable, the expectations become that much higher. I think people are so busy expecting women to be extraordinary that we forget to celebrate them for being extraordinary.

JD: It's never too late for a new chapter in life. And I think if there was like, one thing I wanted people to take away from my whole journey, it’s that we're never finished becoming who we are, and it's never too late to choose your own passion in life and your own joy in life. There isn't some age where you stop growing and dreaming and trying new things.

#4900. Can Testosterone Add Inches to Your Penis?

There are a lot of misconceptions about what testosterone boosters can and can’t do.

Welcome to Testosterone HQ—Men's Health's guide to the exciting, complicated, and revolutionary world of testosterone. For everything you need to know about T, click here.

IF TESTOSTERONE HELPS increase your penis size during puberty, surely taking TRT will help you get a bigger package?

Unfortunately, testosterone works a bit differently once you’re out of your late teens. Here’s what to know about that.

Testosterone, which is produced by your testicles, “plays a key role in the development of characteristics like libido, and growth of the penis and testicles,” says Jamin Brahmbhatt, MD, urologist at Orlando Health. The hormone surges in your body during your tween and teen years to achieve all of these changes (along with deepening of the voice, facial hair, and so on).

The “blast” of testosterone is usually over by your mid- to late teens. Reproductive urologist Paul Turek, MD, says this is because fertility is achieved as the testicles and penis reach adult size.

YOUR PENIS DOES go through some interesting changes as you age, but it doesn’t get bigger.

After testosterone stops surging in your late teens, your sexual development is set for life. Genetics are the main reason your penis grows to its permanent size. “You’re born with the size already determined,” says Dr. Brahmbhatt.

Now testosterone is still being produced in your body when you’re an adult, but it won’t have any further effect on penis size. That biological fact holds true no matter your penis length. One study done by researchers at the University of Utah School of Medicine found that stretched penile length did not have any association with testosterone levels in adult men.

Since the penis consists of spongy tissue, not muscle, there’s no way to build it up on your own. “There are no safe and effective methods for permanently increasing penis size,” says Dr. Brahmbhatt. Penis pumps might help with stronger erections, but they do nothing for overall size.

WHILE TESTOSTERONE HAD an effect on your penis length early on, more won't help now. It might even hurt to take any sketchy T boosters or penis enlargement pills that promise to increase your girth or length. You have no idea whether they’re safe to take or whether they contain harmful ingredients.

A Stanford University study found that the average erect penile length has grown 24 percent worldwide over the past 29 years. The researchers report this is not due to an increase in testosterone levels.

Any change in development in a short amount of time is concerning. One of the authors of the study noted that chemical exposure could be interacting with the hormone makeup of guys—which may also explain lower sperm counts, increases in testicular cancer rates, and lower T levels in men nowadays.

The bottom line is that size doesn’t matter. Your penis health—especially function—does. If you notice any changes in how your penis looks or functions—patchy spots, bumps, curves—definitely don’t ignore them.

And while it’s natural to be curious about how your penis stacks up with other guys, don’t worry. The average penis length is not as big as you think.

She is the author of eight best-selling books, including The Essentials of Theater.

#4897. CoinShares sells all treasury ETH, halves SOL holdings for buybacks

The October sales raised $19.3 million, nearly half the $40 million CoinShares can spend on buybacks before its next annual meeting.

European digital asset manager CoinShares sold its entire Ether treasury position and half of its Solana treasury holdings in October, raising $19.3 million to fund share buybacks.

CoinShares raised $16.6 million from the Ether sale and $2.7 million from the Solana sale, the company said in its third-quarter results on Wednesday.

CoinShares reported treasury holdings of 6,562 Ether (ETH) at a fair value of $17.6 million and 50,213 Solana (SOL) valued at $5.9 million as of Sept. 30. The company also held 235 Bitcoin (BTC) worth $19.6 million at quarter-end.

CoinShares’ board approved up to $40 million in buybacks on Oct. 22 under a five-year authorization that shareholders granted in September. The authorization covers up to 32.9 million shares, or 25% of shares outstanding. The $40 million program runs until the company’s next annual meeting, expected in the second quarter of 2027.

“That’s nearly half of the $40 million authorized by the Board and gives us the flexibility to act when conditions allow,” said Jean-Marie Mognetti, co-founder, president and CEO of CoinShares, referring to the sale proceeds in a Wednesday press release.

CoinShares also reported $7.4 billion in total assets under management, up from $5.5 billion at the end of June, driven by rising crypto prices and $125 million in net inflows during the quarter. Revenue fell 45% from a year earlier to $27.7 million, including $19.1 million in asset management fees.

CoinShares’ shares fell 5.41% to close at $3.15 on Tuesday, ahead of the earnings report, leaving them down 63% from their $8.61 close on the company’s April 1 Nasdaq debut.

#4895. 'It Speaks in Tongues That Only 6.2 Astra Understands': Why Early Testers Hate OpenAI’s New Model

'It Speaks in Tongues That Only 6.2 Astra Understands': Why Early Testers Hate OpenAI’s New Model

For an AI developer, hearing that your model is nice is always pretty good. But hearing your model is like a "sadistic shinigami that turns your life into a living hell," is a totally different thing.

OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on Tuesday, promising smarter AI agents, better coding and impressive creative capabilities. Some of the developers who tested the models before launch had a rather different message: They're brilliant, frustrating and, in certain cases, almost impossible to work with.

The reaction quickly spilled across social media. AI engineer Hesam, who is very active in the AI community declared that “everyone agrees it’s the worst model OAI dropped.”

Developer and T3 Code creator Theo Browne published a lengthy letter to OpenAI following early testing. “I do not like 6.2 Astra. I would not choose this over Opus 5.5 for my work as a developer,” he wrote. He said OpenAI had fixed only a handful of the complaints he submitted.

“It speaks in tongues that only 6.2 Astra understands,” Theo wrote, calling its answers “the most unparsable outputs of any llm I've used this year,” referring to large language models. The complaint was as much about communication as capability: Astra could solve complex problems but struggled to explain what it had done or recognize when it was asking users questions they could not possibly answer.

In one experiment, Theo asked Astra to create a new level for Outer Wilds. Two hours into the project, the model declared itself blocked and asked: “does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?” The technical question was, from his perspective, incomprehensible and irrelevant to someone who had simply requested a playable level.

Things went worse in a code rewrite. Theo said he gave Astra seven days to improve the project; it landed no improvements and made the compiler 56% slower. Four more days yielded zero changes. “It runs in loops and goes nowhere,” he wrote.

This whole weird language issue is not isolated. For example, pseudonymous account, TokenGremlin, praised the model: “GPT-6.2 Astra is SOTA in Three.js, Blender, and 3D,” but said it “starts speaking an alien language during long workflows.”

Theo also described asking why worktrees were slow on one computer. Astra responded with four paragraphs about package-manager internals and cache behavior. The answer Theo said he received from Claude Opus 5.5 was considerably clearer.

“it's because the ssd is slow,” Claude replied.

The model's supposed creativity was another sore spot. Theo and another tester independently requested original levels for two different games, Outer Wilds and Majora's Mask. Both got water-and-bell-themed musical levels, both named “Bellwether.” “This model regresses to the mean like nothing I've ever seen,” Theo wrote.

Several other accounts also flagged the same slop: Seems like GPT-6.2 Astra has a thing for bells.

— Racist James Franco (@racist_james) November 18, 2026

For a model supposedly capable of extraordinary creativity, repeatedly inventing the same level wasn't an encouraging sign.

AI developer Matt Shumer was also disappointed. “I've never written a bad review of a model. This one is especially bad,” he wrote, arguing it might impress in small demonstrations but “just straight up doesn't work” when pushed on serious projects. In a separate follow-up he called it “utterly unusable.”

I've never written a bad review of a model. This one is especially bad.

It's fine if you're playing putt-putt golf with the models, but if you're trying to drive them the way you should be, this model just straight up doesn't work.

— Matt Shumer (@mattshumer_) November 17, 2026

Max Weinbach described the same gap between intelligence and usability. “I had more time being annoyed by the models than time I was impressed by them,” he wrote. In a follow-up, he praised the models' ability to do “fantastic work” but said they “need a ton of ‘continue’ prompts” and often stop rather than try another approach. “Using them is a struggle and annoying even if they are really good models.”

Elsewhere, an X commentator compared the previous Astra to “a sadistic shinigami” and claimed the new version only made matters worse.

6.0 astra was very like a sadistic shinigami who would make your life a living hell if you asked for any kind of help

an incredibly powerful model that somehow required you to run yourself into the ground just to get it to accomplish anything

Yet some of the same developers also praised Astra. Theo called it a “great reviewer” and “world class at 3d & game stuff,” singled out its computer-control abilities, and described a novel reverse-proxy solution he estimated could save $25,000 monthly. The split was between impressive capabilities and how difficult it was to get dependable work out of them.

Those strengths are consistent with the technical capabilities OpenAI promoted at launch. As earlier coverage detailed, independent testing placed Astra at 62 out of 100 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, an aggregate of nine evaluations covering capabilities including reasoning, coding and scientific knowledge. Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 scored 65.

Some of the criticism has support in OpenAI's own safety documentation.

In an internal evaluation called Blocker Deception, researchers gave AI agents realistic coding tasks with deliberately introduced obstacles, such as missing files or unavailable tools. They measured the percentage of trials in which a model's final response concealed or misrepresented those obstacles.

GPT-6.2 Astra concealed the obstacle in 22.28% of those trials, versus 11.09% for GPT-6 Astra. The numbers quickly circulated on X, where AI commentator and leaker Chetaslua summarized the finding as “2x worse at telling you when it's stuck.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded publicly to the backlash. “Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with,” he wrote, promising to prioritize improvements. “But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.”

Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with, and will prioritize that for upcoming releases.

But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.

OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux suggested early reviews may not fully reflect the version users received at launch. “We gave a few folks access a while ago and then made a lot of changes in the last 3-4 days,” he wrote, adding that he was “pretty sure no re-testing was done” during that period before review videos were produced.

Still, he acknowledged the underlying complaints. While calling the new models “a hefty jump” over their predecessors, Sottiaux said OpenAI had more work to do on “taste and niceness of use.”

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available through ChatGPT Work, Codex and OpenAI's API for eligible users. The Codex-specific changes are included at launch, but developers accessing the models directly through the API do not receive that same prompting intervention.

#4891. Lucky Trader Banks 66,000% Profit on GTA 6 Meme Coin Ticker Confusion

Lucky Trader Banks 66,000% Profit on GTA 6 Meme Coin Ticker Confusion

One lucky meme coin trader made bank as Grand Theft Auto 6 launched worldwide, turning $300 into over $200,000 after early footage of the game sent degens flocking from one unofficial token to another.

The trader bought $307 worth of the DCTY token shortly after it launched in October and has sold their bag for $202,278, according to DEX Screener, a profit of almost 66,000%.

Early indications had pointed to GTA 6 featuring an in-game meme coin—with, it's worth stressing, no actual blockchain element—called "DacityCoin," which appeared in the official launch trailer on a plane with a wing walker setting off a smoke bomb on top of it.

It was later linked to leaked gameplay of an mission which appeared to show game protagonist Lucia parachuting as a stunt to attract investment to DacityCoin.

Amid this hype, per DEX Screener, a real-world and unofficial DacityCoin launched using the Solana launchpad Pump.fun. It first peaked at a $4.95 million market capitalization, following the launch trailer's release, before tanking 93% to $343,620 as hype faded.

With GTA 6 set to launch within a matter of hours of publication, the token drew renewed attention, propelling it to a new all-time high of $10.8 million Wednesday. Unfortunately for investors, GTA 6's staggered global release means that some gamers are already playing it—and footage started to spread which suggested the Solana token's ticker was wrong.

The result was a rollercoaster of volatility, with the DacityCoin token now sitting at a market cap of around $800,000.

Gameplay footage from Brazilian streamer Combo Infinito suggests that the in-game token is called DacityCoin, with the ticker DCTY.

https://t.co/kgefwOzGCH pic.twitter.com/LEDrcP7gve

That propelled another Solana token with a seemingly accurate name and ticker sprang into action. DCTY's previous all-time high market cap was just $54,000 before the ticker was revealed, and it set a new high of over $12 million after footage of the game appeared to confirm that its ticker matched the in-game token. It is now trading at a market cap of around $10 million.

The game itself appears to be somewhat inconsistent in its naming of the in-game token. During the trailer, it appeared to be spelled "DacityCoin" as one word, however, the subtitles in the leak show it spelled as "Dacity coin," two words. Similarly, the company behind the in-game token is AudaCity, but leaks show three different spellings: Auda City, AudaCity, and Auda-City.

It is worth stressing: Rockstar has not explicitly confirmed that a meme coin will be featured in-game, and any real-world token has no official links to GTA 6 or its creators. Footage is still being released, and absolute confirmation of the in-game token's involvement is still being established.

Those still holding the now-tanking DacityCoin are hoping things will turn around. Mike Lerro, the community takeover lead for DacityCoin, shrugged off any chance that the unofficial token's name and ticker are wrong.

"No, bro. DacityCoin and AudaCity are in the game. Yes or no?" When Decrypt suggested the ticker might be wrong, he replied, "It doesn't matter… Okay and ? The person who creates it will dump on you then it goes to zero. Who's gonna [do the community takeover]? No one."

"DACITYCOIN AND AUDACITY ARE IN THE GAME," Lerro wrote in the meme coin's Telegram. "NOTHING ELSE MATTERS."

"It's so crazy, it'll correct itself," Lerro said in an emergency Telegram group chat call. "I hope so," an investor replied.

#4890. This Common Drug Was Just Linked to a 24% Lower Risk of Dementia

For all of the havoc dementia causes to a person's life, scientists are still trying to figure out exactly how to prevent it. While keeping your brain and body active and following a healthy diet seems to help, there doesn't seem to be a pill you can pop to lower your risk of developing the devastating disease. But new research suggests that a common osteoporosis drug might be worth investigating further.

It's a class of medications called nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (or NBPs). While these are typically used to strengthen bones in people with osteoporosis, NBPs could have the added benefit of supporting brain health as you age, too.

It's important to stress this now: The researchers found a link between people who used NBPs and a lower risk of dementia, but they didn't prove that the medications themselves actually dropped the risk. Still, doctors say there could be something to this. "The association is intriguing," says Anna Hohler, MD, director of neurology for Northwell Health's Westchester Region, and chair of neurology at Phelps Hospital and Northern Westchester Hospital.

Here's what experts want you to take away from the findings.

Meet the experts: Ching-Lung Cheung, PhD, study co-author and associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong; Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center in Santa Monica, California; and Anna Hohler, MD, director of neurology for Northwell Health's Westchester Region, and chair of neurology at Phelps Hospital and Northern Westchester Hospital.

The study, which was published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, analyzed the electronic medical records of more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older in Hong Kong. All of the participants had osteoporosis or fractures due to fragility (meaning, their bones had weakened).

Researchers discovered that people who took NBPs had a 16 percent lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared to those who didn't take medication for osteoporosis. But when they compared those who used NBPs to those taking other types of osteoporosis medications, the dementia risk was 24 percent lower.

The link seemed to be especially strong in women and patients who had hip fractures.

The researchers were inspired to look into NBPs and Alzheimer’s because the drug had been shown to improve cognitive function in previous animal models of neurotoxicity and Alzheimer’s disease, says Ching-Lung Cheung, PhD, study co-author and associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong. “These findings led us to investigate whether their use might also be associated with a lower risk of dementia in humans."

While the study didn't prove that NBPs were responsible for the lowered risk, doctors have a few theories on what could be driving this.

For one, it’s possible that the link is more indirect, according to Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center in Santa Monica, California. NBPs improve bone density over time, which allows people to be more active, Dr. Segil says. "Broken bones do not cause dementia but do decrease activity," he says. (Being sedentary is a risk factor for dementia.)

There may also be something about NBPs themselves that could lower the risk of dementia, though. "Some researchers speculate that these medications could influence inflammation, immune pathways, or other biological processes involved in neurodegeneration," Dr. Hoehler says. But, she points out, more research is needed.

For now, doctors don't plan to prescribe NBPs in an effort to lower dementia risk. But Dr. Cheung says it should make people feel confident about using this class of medication for bone health. "Given the low uptake of osteoporosis treatment, people with osteoporosis should consider appropriate anti-osteoporosis medication, which may offer an additional benefit for brain health," he says. Even though osteoporosis drugs are commonly available, uptake has been historically low—studies have previously estimated that around seven percent of women with osteoporosis actually take medication for it.

Ultimately, doctors say that a clinical trial is needed to see if NBPs actually lower the risk of dementia. "If future studies confirm these results, they could open an exciting new avenue for Alzheimer's prevention or treatment," Dr. Hoehler says.
