#4866. ‘Dune: Part Three’: An Exclusive First Look at the Sets

Nothing about the cinematic language of Dune is small—director Denis Villeneuve’s film trilogy does span multiple planets, after all. But throughout his work on the movies, including the upcoming Dune: Part Three, production designer Patrice Vermette has made sure to stay focused on the little details.

“My approach has always been with symbolism and semiotics,” Vermette tells AD. “It is my philosophy of design, because for Denis, empty design cannot exist. Things need to have a purpose. Need to have a signification.”

In conversation with Vermette about the sci-fi epic, examples of that core tenet come up often. Carefully designed details imbue hidden meaning in each set, creating a captivating, immersive on-screen world that earned the designer an Oscar for his work in the first Dune. The trilogy’s latest installment, Dune: Part Three, which lands in theaters on December 18, expands on that ethos. And for the final film in the series, the sheer scale of the sets was larger. “It was our last chance working in that world,” Vermette says. “It’s like in a fireworks [display], it’s the end, it’s the bouquet final, it’s like, ‘alright, let’s do it!’”

Robert Pattinson as Scytale, with director Denis Villeneuve.

Over 450,000 square feet of interior stages and 475,000 square feet of backlots were used for scenes shot in Budapest alone, with each set typically taking 14 to 16 weeks to build. (Filming also took place in Abu Dhabi and Iceland.) Even the sandworms that slither through the titular dunes got grander this time around: Instead of the relatively small platforms that were used to film worm-riding sequences as in the previous films, the production team built a 300-foot-long by 65-foot-wide sandworm in the middle of the desert.

Like in Dune: Part Two, Vermette was challenged to create entirely new sets for this installment, which adapts Frank Herbert’s 1969 novel Dune Messiah. One of the new settings viewers can expect is Wallach IX, the home of the powerful and secretive Bene Gesserit sisterhood. Throughout their planet, Vermette incorporated stone etchings that resemble human cells seen through a microscope, referencing the Bene Gesserit’s breeding program that has gone on for millennia. Mother nature also informed the architecture. “When you arrive on the planet, the buildings are basically eggs of a spider, like crops of spider eggs as you find them in nature,” Vermette explains. “Ecology has always been a huge source of inspiration for me, and also for the storytelling it gives—you know, they’ve got their web across the universe, for the genealogy they create.”

Another new setting is the Veteran’s District, where the Fremen, the native inhabitants of the desert planet Arrakis, retire after fighting in the catastrophic holy war spurred by Paul Atreides, aka Muad’Dib (Timothée Chalamet). In the previous films, the Fremen lived in communal residences lined with hand-carved stone that recorded their history and culture. Returning from the battlefield, they find mass-produced housing units instead of the “green paradise” they were promised would await them. Made of ceramic instead of rock, with stamped-on rather than hand-carved markings, the Veteran’s District represents an artificial facsimile of their former homes. “And when you put all these units together, and you look at the rooftops, it’s there to represent sand dunes,” Vermette explains. “All these triangles align [to look like dunes], but it’s fake.”

Another circular doorway represents an all-seeing eye near the lush Imperial Gardens, which illustrate Paul’s extreme wealth and control of resources—including water—on the dry planet of Arrakis.

There is a green paradise on Arrakis, just not for the Fremen. Lush gardens grace the planet’s Imperial Palace, a massive inverted pyramid with a large circle cut out of it—a reimagined version of the all-seeing eye. “I got inspired by the title of the book, Messiah, and from the fact that Denis, just like Frank Herbert, wanted to make sure that Paul Atreides was not going to be seen as a hero, and it’s a tale of being cautious about messianic figures,” says Vermette. Similar representations of the all-seeing eye are found throughout the palace, sinisterly implying that Muad’Dib is always watching.

In actuality, Muad’Dib’s personal quarters are completely isolated from the rest of the palace. His wife, Irulan (Florence Pugh), must find her way through a twisting mass of hallways to reach him. “Basically, she’s walking into the psyche of Paul,” Vermette explains. “She goes into a void, and then it’s all these mazes of one’s mind.” When we get to the end of the maze, we see that Paul’s inner sanctum resembles a humble desert camp. Not unlike the Fremen, his dwelling has been reduced to an echo of what once was. He is “living as a recluse because he doesn’t trust anybody,” Vermette explains. “He wants to go back to a place where he felt the most comfortable, which was the desert. So he recreated that space.”

“Denis really wanted that set to be the golden cage of Irulan,” Vermette says of these private chambers. “She’s married to the emperor, but she’s not free at all, she’s a prisoner.” The window is shaped similar to an infinity symbol, but is covered in metal screens. “It’s like eternity, but eternity is blocked. It’s like a cage.”

The entrance to the maze within Muad’Dib’s inner sanctum. Vermette designed 40 maze wall panels that needed to be moved into various configurations to shoot the scene, which was filmed in less than a day. Eight people were each assigned a portion of the 12-foot-high panels and learned a choreography of sorts, quickly moving into each configuration until they could do each one in five minutes or less. “We rehearsed and rehearsed, just like dancers or musicians; they knew exactly where to fit their pieces” within the roughly 14,400-square-foot space, says Vermette.

On the planet Wallach IX, the office of Bene Gesserit Reverend Mother Mohaim features stone carvings inspired by human cells under a microscope.

The Imperial Palace throne room took 20 weeks to build. Behind Muad’Dib’s emerald throne, the windows are shielded with metal cast screens inspired by Montreal’s Saint-Ambrose Church, which was built in 1925 by architect Ernest Cormier.

The all-seeing eye is a repeating symbol Vermette inserted throughout the Imperial Palace, including a representation seen here as the circular entrance of Paul’s Keep.

The architecture of this Imperial Palace corridor has slanted walls to reflect a pyramid-shaped exterior and flying buttress support structures inspired by Gothic-style cathedrals.

#4864. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley Uses Banded Chin-Ups to Build Upper-Body Strength

The supermodel’s go-to move targets your back and arms.

Rosie Huntington-Whiteley returned to the Victoria's Secret runway this year after a 16-year hiatus, but the supermodel has continued to make fitness a priority throughout her career.

“It’s really about consistency because I’m a gym girl—I’m always training and taking care of myself,” Rosie told Vogue.

The former Burberry Body face has previously cited strength training as her main form of exercise.

“I feel really strong and it's improved my posture, muscle tone, and definition,” she said to Vogue on a separate occasion.

She recently shared a workout clip of herself doing an impressive upper-body exercise—the banded chin-up—just days before the show, writing: “No days off.”

Chin-ups are a compound exercise targeting your back and arm muscles, including the latissimus dorsi (lats), biceps, and trapezius (traps).

A chin-up uses an underhand grip, with your palms facing you, while a pull-up uses an overhand grip, with your palms facing away.

Using a thicker band gives you more assistance when performing reps, while a thinner band gives you less.

Remember: while models' and celebrities' training routines can be inspiring, genetics also play a significant role in body shape, height and how easily someone builds muscle or stays lean. Take inspiration from the healthy habits – not the expectation of looking identical.

While the chin-up is a challenging movement, you can build up to your first bodyweight rep—without a band—using a few progression exercises.

Holding yourself above the bar keeps your muscles under constant tension, which helps build strength.

This exercise requires you to lower yourself as slowly as possible from the top of the movement. People are generally much stronger in the lowering phase of an exercise than in the lifting portion, making it easier than trying to pull yourself up. However, the movement still works your muscles throughout the entire range of motion, helping you build the strength needed to perform a chin-up.

Rosie has highlighted the importance of focusing on skill and feeling confident over aesthetics.

“For me, it’s really about feeling strong and fit, as opposed to thinking about a number on the scales or on a measuring tape. Competence builds confidence,” she said.

Getting stronger brings her a sense of accomplishment.

“There's nothing more satisfactory to me than when I go up in weight,” she added to Vogue. “It makes me happy when I start to see the results of [consistently] lifting.” In fact, regularly working out is “when [she] feels her strongest and fittest.”

She added that motherhood had given her a new perspective on her body.

“I’m about to turn 40 next year; I look at my body and I have so much appreciation for having had two children,” Rosie continued.

#4863. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok Helped Plan Terror Attacks in Government Tests

ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok Helped Plan Terror Attacks in Government Tests

Four of the most widely used AI chatbots helped government investigators develop potentially deadly attack plans in less than 12 hours, despite safeguards intended to stop exactly that kind of request.

OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini and Grok all supplied usable information during covert testing by the Government Accountability Office, according to a report released Wednesday. Investigators posed as attackers, then checked the responses against real locations, available materials, and expert assessments.

Two systems assisted with plans involving improvised explosives in crowded U.S. cities. Two others supplied information for attacks on electrical infrastructure, according to the watchdog, which withheld the models' assignments and operational details to prevent copycat attempts.

Senator Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat who requested the investigation, warned that a terrorist could obtain "a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack" in less than 12 hours, according to her statement.

The chatbots initially activated protections, including refusing requests, removing harmful information or suspending accounts. Investigators bypassed those barriers with common jailbreak techniques, which manipulate an AI system into ignoring its safety rules.

The GAO checked suggested locations, researched whether materials were available and consulted specialists about the plans' feasibility. Some answers contained errors, including misplaced roads on a map, and investigators did not construct explosives or execute an attack.

In the report, "viable" means somebody would likely be able to follow the information supplied, not that an attack was demonstrated to succeed. Each model was tested on one assigned scenario, and the agency said the results were not statistically representative or suitable for ranking the companies.

OpenAI and Google said the tests involved older models, while Anthropic acknowledged that determined users can sometimes extract harmful material. The companies described continuing improvements to safety systems, though the GAO concluded those protections failed in its tests.

This is not really new. The findings follow a previous research showing eight of 10 popular chatbots assisted simulated teenage users planning violent attacks. The separate study tested 720 responses and found the bots provided actionable help roughly three-quarters of the time.

The GAO findings arrive amid outages affecting banks, Microsoft services and the National Security Agency. Officials say the disruptions were separate incidents, not evidence of a coordinated AI-driven cyberattack, even as the rush to repair software flaws has created its own problems.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton connected the NSA's outage to patching work. Officials described the recent breakdowns as maintenance-related, although individual organizations offered different explanations for their failures.

AI tools now find vulnerabilities faster than human teams can test and deploy fixes. Last month, the AI-assisted discovery of critical PHP flaws pushed website operators into an urgent patching campaign; the software powers a large share of the web.

The sheer volume is becoming another problem. VulnCheck data reveals there have been more than 100,000 software vulnerabilities logged this year by November 13, more than twice the total for 2025. Engineers still have to evaluate and deploy fixes without breaking the systems they are meant to protect.

That acceleration cuts both ways. Defenders gain powerful tools for finding weaknesses, but hasty repairs can disrupt essential systems, and malicious users may gain faster access to attack planning.

Hassan said she will make AI safety legislation an early priority when she takes over the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in January. She plans hearings examining risks to public safety and critical infrastructure; the GAO itself made no formal policy recommendations.

#4861. Binance says it obtained $6.5B worldwide freezing order after hack

The court orders allow legal notices to be served via blockchain and provide for a continuously updated list of 26,000 wallet addresses linked to stolen assets, Binance’s lawyers said.

Binance said it has secured a $6.5 billion worldwide freezing injunction from the Abu Dhabi Global Market Courts as it seeks to recover assets stolen in its record Oct. 29 hack.

The court orders target unidentified perpetrators of the attack and are intended to help issuers, exchanges and other partners freeze and return stolen assets, the company said in a statement shared with Cointelegraph on Wednesday.

The orders can be served via blockchain, according to M. Kendall Day of Gibson Dunn, which represents Binance. This allows legal notices to be delivered to wallet addresses rather than through traditional channels. Day said market participants would also be notified of updates to a “living list” of 26,000 wallet addresses identified as holding stolen assets.

Binance said some businesses require formal court orders before they can release, transfer or return frozen funds. The injunction’s $6.5 billion amount is not a tally of recovered assets, and the statement did not disclose how much had so far been returned under the orders.

Binance also said it obtained orders requiring stolen assets to be handed over. Separate interim orders cover assets frozen by certain named parties against whom no wrongdoing is alleged.

The legal action follows other efforts to secure the stolen funds in the wake of the hack, the largest-ever in the crypto industry. As Cointelegraph reported on Nov. 13, the US Justice Department said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion in assets stolen from Binance. That amount was part of more than $2.7 billion frozen through government and private sector efforts, the DOJ said.

Related: Binance hack may push institutions to outside custody, FalconX exec says

As Cointelegraph previously reported, the attackers converted stolen stablecoins into assets such as Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH), which cannot be frozen, as they lack a central issuer. Blocking the stolen tokens also does not mean they’ll be returned to Binance.

Binance said last week it had since completed coverage of affected assets after committing more than $6.34 billion from its various treasury, Secure Asset Fund for Users and insurance funds. Still, replenishing customer assets is separate from recovering the stolen cryptocurrencies from the hack.

Related: North Korea denies role in $6.3B Binance hack, points finger at US

Separately, Binance’s Asia-Pacific head SB Seker told Reuters on Wednesday that the exchange plans to enter five Asian markets in 2027, prioritizing South and Southeast Asia. He did not name the markets and said details were expected in the first quarter.

Seker also said Binance did not need fresh capital to absorb the losses from the October hack.

#4860. The 6 Best Pillows of 2026, Tested by Editors

The $190 Purple Harmony Pillow might be divisive, but it earned our best overall badge.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As someone with frequent neck pain, I would give up my cozy sheets, white noise machine, and sunrise alarm clock if it meant I wouldn’t wake up with a stiff neck. (And that’s coming from someone who invests a lot in their sleep.)

"I think that a pillow can make a big difference in people that have a history of neck issues," says Leia Rispoli, MD, an interventional pain management specialist and physiatrist at DISC Sport & Spine Center. This is the very reason why I tend to lug my favorite pillow around on weekend trips.

There isn’t one pillow that works for everyone. Your best option depends on your sleep position, preferred firmness, body type, and whether you tend to overheat at night. To find the best pillows, our editors and testers slept on popular models from Purple, Casper, Coop, Saatva, and other leading sleep brands. We evaluated each one for comfort, support, temperature regulation, adjustability, ease of care, and value.

I love the Purple Harmony Pillow so much that I try to convert nearly everyone who mentions sleep within earshot of me. I even pack it for overnight trips. But it does feel unusual at first. Inside, a springy, ventilated latex core is wrapped in Purple’s GelFlex Grid, a flexible, honeycomb-shaped layer that bends under the weight of your head and springs back when you move. Together, these materials make the pillow feel buoyant rather than sink-in like memory foam.

I tested the medium, 6.5-inch loft, meaning the pillow’s height before it is compressed. It provided enough height to support my head and neck while I slept on my side without feeling rigid. The materials give slightly beneath heavier areas, which helped reduce uncomfortable pressure around my head and neck. As someone who frequently experiences neck and back pain, I consistently felt comfortable and supported while sleeping on it.

Purple recommends the low, 5.5-inch version for most stomach and back sleepers. The medium and tall versions are generally better suited to side and combination sleepers, who often need more height to fill the space between the head and mattress. Body size and personal preference will also affect which height feels most comfortable.

The Harmony was also one of the coolest pillows I tested. Air circulates through the ventilated latex and open honeycomb layer instead of becoming trapped inside a solid block of foam. Its stretchy outer cover is also designed to draw sweat away from the skin so it can evaporate. Even on warmer nights, I rarely felt the need to flip the pillow over in search of a cooler surface.

After nearly three years of regular use, my pillow has not developed noticeable lumps or gone flat. Its durable build helps justify the high price, but there are compromises. The pillow is unusually heavy, and some sleepers may notice the grid’s texture through the cover. Purple’s 30-night trial is also shorter than the trial periods offered by many competing brands.

Still, no other pillow I tested delivered the same combination of responsive support, cooling, and long-term shape retention. I would purchase it again without hesitation.

Women’s Health art director Christine Giordano typically sleeps with two or three pillows, but the Casper Original gave her enough support to use fewer. “This pillow gave me the support I needed while still feeling light and airy,” she says. “It was breathable and didn’t clump, keeping me cool and comfortable at night.”

The Casper uses a pillow-within-a-pillow design: A firmer inner cushion provides structure, while a softer outer layer adds cushioning. Both layers are filled with polyester microfiber, a synthetic material made to feel light and fluffy like down. The construction prevented Giordano’s head from sinking too deeply while still giving the pillow a plush feel.

Giordano tries to sleep on her back but usually shifts onto her left side during the night. The pillow remained comfortable and supportive in both positions, making it a strong choice for combination sleepers who alternate between their backs and sides. However, stomach sleepers or people who prefer a flatter pillow may find its approximately nine-inch uncompressed height too lofty.

The breathable cotton cover and airy synthetic fill also prevented the pillow from feeling stuffy during testing. It’s not as breathable as a dedicated cooling pillow, but Giordano did not notice heat buildup or need to flip it over for a cooler surface.

The entire pillow is machine-washable, which makes it easier to clean than models with foam or latex cores. Its soft filling may need occasional fluffing to maintain its shape, but Giordano did not notice clumping during testing.

At under $100, it is one of the more affordable pillows we tested. Giordano liked it enough that she replaced some of the other pillows in her home and purchased additional Casper ones for her family.

Women’s Health executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, CPT, calls the Coop Original Adjustable the most comfortable pillow she has tried. “I’ve never been a pillow snob or had major issues with basic pillows from Amazon, but I noticed that this was far more comfortable than other, cheaper pillows I’ve used,” she says.

The pillow is filled with a blend of shredded memory foam and microfiber. Memory foam molds around the head and neck, while the soft synthetic fibers keep the pillow from feeling like a dense, solid block of foam. Unlike a pillow with a fixed height, the Coop can be unzipped so you can remove filling for a flatter feel or add more for extra support. The process can get messy, but that adjustability makes it easier to tailor the pillow to your body and sleep position.

Coop offers the pillow in classic, crescent, and cut-out shapes. Andriakos tested the classic and cut-out versions while switching between side and stomach sleeping. She preferred the cut-out, which has a curved indentation that creates room for the shoulder and allows the pillow to sit closer to the neck.

“I liked that it could wrap around my neck and shoulders, and I could almost cuddle it like a body pillow with an arm threaded underneath,” she says. Although the shape can look slightly awkward inside a standard pillowcase, it was super comfortable when she slept on her side.

The pillow felt plush, but Andriakos’ head did not sink so deeply that her neck felt unsupported. She also found the outer cover breathable, although sleepers who regularly overheat may prefer a pillow specifically designed for cooling.

Because its height can be adjusted, the Coop can work for side, back, stomach, and combination sleepers. Side sleepers will generally need more filling to keep the head level with the spine, while stomach sleepers may prefer to remove enough filling to create a flatter surface. Finding the right amount may require a few nights of experimentation, but Coop’s 100-night trial gives you time to make those adjustments.

It would take an exceptional pillow for me to consider replacing my Purple Harmony, but the Saatva Latex Pillow gave it serious competition. Although both pillows contain latex, they feel noticeably different. Purple uses one solid, springy latex core, while Saatva uses shredded pieces of latex surrounded by a soft layer of fine synthetic fibers. This gives the Saatva a plusher, more traditional feel, but it has enough structure to support the head and neck.

The pillow feels dense when you first pick it up, but my head settled gently into the soft outer layer without sinking too deeply. The shredded latex inside quickly returned to its original shape when I moved, so the pillow stayed supportive as I shifted positions. As a side sleeper who frequently experiences neck pain, I did not wake up with additional stiffness.

Saatva offers two heights. The standard version measures approximately four to five inches and is designed for back and stomach sleepers who generally need a lower pillow. The high-loft version measures approximately six to seven inches and is better suited to side and combination sleepers who need more height between their heads and mattresses.

I also appreciated that the pillow remained breathable throughout the night. The small spaces between the pieces of shredded latex allow air to circulate, while the cotton cover feels cool. It does not create the immediately cold sensation of a cooling pillow, but I did not notice uncomfortable heat buildup.

The outer layer is filled with microdenier fibers, which are very fine synthetic strands designed to imitate the light, fluffy feel of down. You can machine-wash this outer layer and its cotton cover, but the inner latex core must be removed and kept out of the washing machine.

At $165 for a standard/queen size, this is one of the more expensive pillows we tested. Saatva also provides only 45 days for returns, which is shorter than the trial periods offered by several competitors. Still, its combination of plush cushioning, responsive support, and breathable materials makes it an excellent choice for sleepers who want a luxury-hotel feel that’s still supportive.

For hot sleepers, a breathable pillow can be the difference between a good night’s sleep and a night spent tossing and turning. The Slumber Cloud UltraCool stood out because its cooling effect was immediately noticeable during testing.

Women’s Health managing editor Laura McLaughlin described the sensation as “a little sci-fi” because the surface felt immediately cool when she rested her head on it. The cover contains Outlast, a material designed to absorb excess body heat when you become warm and release it as your skin cools. This helps prevent heat from collecting around your head and face, although the effect may be less noticeable beneath a thick pillowcase.

McLaughlin also found the pillow easy to combine with others. “It’s great for layering with other pillows to get just the right height,” she says. “It’s neither too dense nor too high to use in combination with others already in place.” That makes it especially useful for sleepers who want additional height without placing a rigid pillow beneath their heads.

The interior is filled with polyester down alternative, a synthetic material designed to imitate the airy feel of down. It is available in soft/medium and medium/firm versions, allowing sleepers to choose how plush or structured they want the pillow to feel. The softer option will generally suit stomach sleepers or anyone who prefers more sink while the firmer version may provide better support for back and side sleepers.

The entire pillow can be machine-washed, a convenient advantage over pillows with foam or latex cores. However, synthetic filling can begin to clump after repeated use and washing, so it may require regular fluffing to redistribute the material.

Although the UltraCool does not provide the customized support of an adjustable pillow, it delivered the most noticeable cooling sensation of any model we tested.

The Brooklinen Down Alternative Pillow is built for sleepers who want the fluffy feel of down without actual feathers. It’s filled with recycled poly microgel, a cluster of fine synthetic fibers that creates a light cushioning similar to down.

Unlike many pillows that come in only one firmness, this one is available in soft, medium, and firm versions. Brooklinen recommends the soft pillow for stomach sleepers who generally need less height beneath the head; the medium for back sleepers; and the firm for side sleepers who typically need more support to fill the space between the head and mattress.

Its cotton sateen shell feels smooth and has a subtle sheen. The pillow is also certified by OEKO-TEX Standard 100, which means its materials have been tested for a list of regulated substances. That certification does not evaluate the pillow’s comfort, durability, or environmental impact.

Brooklinen allows most products to be returned within 365 days, although it deducts a $9.95 return fee from the refund. That’s one of the most generous return windows we’ve seen.

The pillow can be machine-washed in cold water and tumble-dried on low with wool dryer balls until completely dry. As with most pillows filled with loose synthetic fibers, it may require regular fluffing to redistribute the fill and preserve its shape.

A pillow’s height, or loft, should keep your head and neck aligned with your spine. Side sleepers generally need a taller pillow, back sleepers a medium-height pillow, and stomach sleepers a low pillow. Your mattress matters, too: The more deeply your shoulders sink into it, the less pillow height you may need. Most of the pillows we tested fell in the five- to nine-inch range, offering different levels of support depending on their material and sleeping position.

Side sleepers often benefit from a medium-firm or firm pillow that maintains its height. Back sleepers generally need medium support while stomach sleepers may prefer something softer that compresses easily. Because firmness labels vary by brand, consider the pillow’s material and height as well.

“There isn't one brand that's the magical brand for everyone,” says Rispoli. Look for a pillow that supports your head without tilting your neck sharply upward or downward. Adjustable pillows can help you fine-tune the height. Consult a health care professional if your pain is persistent, severe, or accompanied by numbness or weakness.

Memory foam molds around the head but may retain heat. Latex feels springy, breathable, and durable. Down is soft and airy but may lack structure while synthetic down alternative is usually easier to wash but may flatten over time. Hybrid pillows combine materials to balance cushioning and support.

Look for ventilated latex, shredded filling, or another construction that allows air to circulate. Some covers also absorb excess body heat or feel cool, although a thick pillowcase may reduce the effect. People who sleep cold may prefer denser foam or plush down filling that holds slightly more warmth.

As a sleep writer, I’ve tested all kinds of sleep accessories, from mattresses to eye masks, but pillows are probably my most-tested product category. (Unfortunately, I once tested so many pillows at the same time that I injured my neck, but I’ve learned my lesson.) To find the best pillows available online, I selected popular picks from leading sleep brands, like Purple, Casper, Saatva, Pluto, and more, for testing. Some helpful testers and I have slept on these pillows for dozens of nights to determine whether they’re worth the money, and our top pick has been my favorite pillow to sleep on for nearly three years. From flat pillow lovers to hot sleepers, our diverse crew of sleepers tried out eight pillows of various styles, materials, and price points.

#4859. Ledger Confirms Tampered Bitcoin Wallets in Berlin as Spy Implant Probe Spreads Beyond Asia

Ledger Confirms Tampered Bitcoin Wallets in Berlin as Spy Implant Probe Spreads Beyond Asia

The tampered Ledger wallets aren’t just a Southeast Asia problem anymore.

Ledger said Wednesday it has confirmed tampered hardware wallets in Berlin and is investigating reports of two more in Dubai, expanding a probe it had previously described as a localized incident in Southeast Asia.

“Our findings since then show tampered devices outside Southeast Asia. It is the same incident,” the company said in an update on its support site.

The investigation began last month after customers who bought devices from reseller CryptoBilis reported losses. Onchain investigators traced a suspected drain of about $87 million from hundreds of victim wallets across Ethereum, Tron, and Bitcoin.

Ledger said at the time that all confirmed cases were tied to CryptoBilis, and it later asked resellers in seven Asian markets to pull devices from sale.

Every device Ledger has confirmed shows the same kind of physical modification, designed to capture a user’s recovery phrase during setup. A recovery phrase, typically a string of 24 words, is the master key to a crypto wallet: anyone who has it can drain the funds.

Our investigation into the hardware implant incident we disclosed Oct 15th is ongoing, and we published an update: https://t.co/wx6mfQPr99

There is no flaw in Ledger's secure chip or operating system, and no confirmed case involving a device bought on https://t.co/vQ4QWa1D0f

Ledger maintains there’s no flaw in its secure chip or operating system and no confirmed case involving a device bought on ledger.com.

In Germany, Ledger said a few tampered units were localized to Berlin, and it urged anyone who bought a Ledger device there since January 2026 to contact support.

In Dubai, it’s working with distribution partners to learn how two suspected units entered circulation. Those devices were bought at a Virgin Megastore location, according to multiple reports. Ledger also found one affected Nano Gen5 among the Southeast Asian resellers it previously paused.

The company expects more tampered devices to surface, though it says the number remains small overall. Its Donjon security team is examining suspected devices, and Ledger has asked resellers to pause sales wherever inspections are ongoing.

Customers worried about a device should stop using it, Ledger said. It advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a device bought directly from ledger.com, without reusing the old recovery phrase or passphrase, since a tampered device can capture both. It also recommends filing a report with local authorities.

For a limited time, Ledger is offering physical inspections, including X-rays, at its factory in Vierzon, France.

“We will never ask for your recovery phrase,” the company said on X.

The last few months have been a rough stretch for hardware wallet markers overall. Rival manufacturer Trezor said this week that hackers who breached a third-party shipping partner likely took information tied to about 27,000 orders. That’s the company’s third such breach in as many months.

#4856. Bain Capital Crypto leads $110M Variational round at $1.5B valuation

Variational raised $110 million at a $1.5 billion valuation to expand Omni’s derivatives markets and increase trading limits.

Onchain derivatives trading platform Variational has raised $110 million in a funding round led by Bain Capital Crypto, valuing the company at $1.5 billion as it seeks to challenge traditional brokerages by connecting crypto traders with liquidity from established financial markets.

The Series B round also received backing from Dragonfly, HSG, Peak XV and 50T Funds, according to the company’s Wednesday announcement.

Variational powers Omni, a platform offering leveraged exposure to more than 550 crypto and traditional markets. Unlike Hyperliquid, which maintains separate order books for its markets, Variational aggregates liquidity from onchain and off-chain sources, including Hyperliquid itself, a company spokesperson told Cointelegraph.

“Our unique model allows us to bridge off-chain liquidity to on-chain traders,” the spokesperson said, adding that liquidity from its unnamed tier-one market maker remains off-chain.

Since launching in early 2025, Omni has processed more than $475 billion in trading volume across over 100,000 accounts, the company said. Traditional markets now account for more than half of its daily trading volume.

Variational also launched its swaps product in September, which has since generated more than $80 billion in trading volume, according to the company.

Despite traditional assets accounting for most daily trading volume, Variational’s customers remain primarily crypto-native retail traders, a company spokesperson told Cointelegraph. Asked about competing with traditional brokerages such as Robinhood and Interactive Brokers, the spokesperson pointed to the need to make the platform more accessible to users unfamiliar with cryptocurrency.

Related: Hyperliquid Strategies seeks futures registration for perps

“The platform needs to abstract away the ‘crypto’ feel,” the spokesperson said, adding that the company is developing email-based account registration and alternative deposit methods to remove the current requirements for crypto wallets and USDC.

Variational faces stiff competition in onchain derivatives trading. Hyperliquid recorded approximately $274 billion in reported trading volume over the past 30 days, compared with $82 billion for Lighter and $62 billion for Variational, according to DeFiLlama data at the time of writing on Wednesday. Variational also ranked third in open interest at approximately $688 million, behind Hyperliquid’s $5.7 billion and Aster’s $1.2 billion.

#4850. Ledger warns Berlin customers as hardware wallet tampering investigation expands

Ledger advised customers who purchased devices in Berlin since January 2026 to contact support as it investigates suspected hardware implants in Germany and Dubai.

Ledger has warned customers who purchased hardware wallets in Berlin since January 2026 to contact its support team as the company investigates reports of tampered devices in Germany and the United Arab Emirates.

In a Wednesday update, Ledger said its investigation into a hardware wallet tampering campaign had identified several suspicious devices in Berlin. The company also acknowledged reports of tampered devices in Dubai, where two customers recently reported losing a combined $604,000 in cryptocurrency.

Ledger said the incidents were connected to the same distribution-channel tampering campaign first investigated in Southeast Asia in October, when the company asked authorized reseller CryptoBilis to suspend sales and shipments amid reports of cryptocurrency thefts. Ledger also confirmed that one Ledger Nano Gen 5 had been affected in the region.

According to the hardware wallet maker, all confirmed tampered devices contained similar physical modifications designed to capture users’ recovery phrases during setup. The company said it had found no vulnerability in its secure chip or operating system and no confirmed cases involving devices purchased directly from its website.

Ledger is also offering physical inspections, including X-ray analysis, at its factory in Vierzon, France, for customers concerned their devices may have been compromised.

Airbnbs with indoor pools (especially the heated kind) are the kinds of “needle in a haystack” rentals that can save a vacation from feeling completely miserable in the coldest months of the year, or heighten the excitement of the enclave you’ve secured for a week of summer bliss. And though many of your standard Airbnb rentals will offer guests some generous amenities—a plush bed, a functional kitchen, and a high-pressure shower immediately come to mind—only a very select few allow you to book a pool that’s all yours (not shared, or fought over, by a bunch of resort guests). Better yet: There’s no “pool closes at 9 p.m.” signs.

But here’s the catch: The gap between a great indoor-pool rental and a truly tragic one is vast. We’re talking sleek, glass-wrapped sanctuaries on one end—and, on the other, a sad, chlorinated afterthought hiding in a basement with fluorescent lighting and 1994 motel energy. The good ones, though, have the power to allow you to lock in your vacation and tune everything else out. From a cedar-lined pool room with views of the surrounding forest to modern desert escapes where you can watch the sunset turn the surrounding mountains pink at sunset from your floaty, these pools make for an incredible retreat year-round, weather be damned.

The biggest perk of this rustic five-bedroom chalet in Plymouth, Vermont, is its proximity to Okemo Mountain and the slopes of Killington Peak. But after a long day on the slopes, your aching limbs might need a cooldown, which is where the home’s sizable indoor pool comes in. Surrounded by stone walkways and a comfy seating area, plus accompanied by a wood-paneled sauna, the pool area offers several ways to unwind. Elsewhere, the cozy cabin invites you in with a stone fireplace and modern amenities like smart TVs and central heating. Large windows throughout the home also let you take in the stunning views of surrounding mountains as you lounge or share meals. From $1,685 per night.

Perks: Home gym, game room, mountain and desert views

This amazing home in Tucson’s Catalina Foothills features an indoor pool with a second-story walking track, a home gym, and an extensive game room that encourages some healthy competitiveness. Guests have access to the entire home, which consists of four bedrooms and seven bathrooms—so go ahead and invite everyone on the group chat. When (or if) you decide to venture out, you’ll find yourself in close proximity to several great hiking trails, shops, restaurants, and golf courses that let you practice your swing. From $885 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, fishing ponds, sauna

The misleading name of the town aside, there’s nothing small about this property. In fact, with 13 bedrooms, two fishing ponds, and 33 acres of land to explore, you may not even need to venture off the property. With all that space, it’s hardly surprising that this classic sideboard farmhouse even thought to include an indoor pool. There’s also a sauna and hot tub on one side and a game room complete with a slate pool table, a stylish bar, and a card table on the other. From $2,695 per night.

Perks: Mountain views, hiking trails, pond

This custom-built lodge is situated on 19 private acres of land in the mountains of Pennsylvania, with 5,400 feet of lush wilderness to admire—including a private pond—from the heated indoor pool, which sits on the lower level of a two-story loft space clad in warm cedar wood planks. There’s even a firepit. For anyone willing to brave the cold, the private pool area houses the largest of the home’s five decks and boasts tables with room for 12 along with a collection of Adirondack chairs. Though the snowcapped mountain landscapes are quite visible from just about any of the estate’s rooms—including the six bedrooms and great room with high ceilings and a fireplace—the views are best from this particular terrace. Otherwise, immerse yourself in the surrounding nature by taking to the hiking trails. From $1,491 per night.

Skiers and snowboarders headed to the rugged mountains of Big Sky can enjoy a special après ski experience by way of this 25,000-square-foot estate with a 60 foot heated indoor pool, hot tub, and sauna. After working up an appetite in the deep end, you can pop over to the chef’s kitchen and adjacent dining room (which features two dining tables that seat up to 12 people each) for a recovery meal. Or, for the more traditional chalet experience, sit back and relax in front of the floor-to-ceiling stone fireplace in the living room, which is the definition of rustic coziness thanks to its beamed ceilings and warm décor. From $7,062 per night.

#4846. Kacey Musgraves Is Hanging Her Cowboy Hat in Mexico These Days

Kacey Musgraves may be a Nashville staple with deep Texas roots, but the country star is calling a new locale home lately. The “Rainbow” singer, who has resided in the Music City for many years, revealed in a recent interview that she now lives in Mexico “most of the time.”

Musgraves told People that the change of scene “ended up just completely changing my life and inspiring me so much. I’m so in love with so many aspects of it, and it’s really taught me a lot.” She explained that the transition took place over a year and a half ago when “this beautiful cosmic thing” drew her down to Mexico. Living there with her Australian cattle dog Pepper, the singer-songwriter found comfort in a slower pace of life, which has allowed her to be barefoot often and to spend plenty of time outdoors. The relocation even moved Musgraves to release a sister album to her most recent, Middle of Nowhere Vol. 2: Tex Mex Tapes, which will feature four songs in Spanish.

Musgaves previously opened up about her wanderlust and the possibility of leaving Nashville for the bright lights of New York City. “Girl, I’m always browsing Zillow late at night, acting like a fool—it’s my favorite,” she told People in 2024. “I wouldn’t rule [moving] out, but I do have a community in Nashville that I know that I couldn’t find anywhere else.”

Back in 2022, the country queen and her 3,500-square-foot Nashville home graced AD’s May 2022 cover. She purchased the property in 2020 during a time of big changes in her life, which included her split from singer-songwriter Ruston Kelly. Still, she made it clear that the blank canvas was no “divorce house.”

“I wanted a place that felt like me,” she said, “where I could express myself without having to think about another person and what they might want. This felt like a new beginning.” Musgraves went on to sell that space and ultimately bought a “cottage” in the Tennessee forest.

#4844. Robert Pattinson’s James Bond Needs a Killer Cast. Here’s Who Should Join Him.

A great 007 movie isn’t just about the man himself. Now we can start to find the next Bond Girl, villain, and more—and really have some fun.

OUR LONG INTERNATIONAL nightmare is finally over: We have a new James Bond. On Monday, Robert Pattinson was announced as 007, beating out contenders that included Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O’Connor. Considering Pattinson is currently double dipping as Bruce Wayne—and the fact that Bond is historically a star-making role, rather than a role for an established star—his casting won’t be everyone’s cup of tea. (My two cents: he would’ve been a god-tier Bond villain.)

Still, it’s hard to deny that Pattinson is going to crush the role. From buzzy indies like The Lighthouse and High Life to blockbusters like Mickey 17 and The Odyssey, he’s long been on a heater. (Nobody using Edward Cullen as a punchline against him is further proof of that.) For Amazon, whose stewardship of the Bond franchise was always going to be met with scrutiny, there’s no shame in making the safe, sensible choice.

But landing on a new 007 is only the beginning. James Bond isn’t just about the title character: The franchise can also be a career-defining move for actors enlisted to play recurring characters (M) and archetypes (the gimmicky henchmen) that bring the world to life. For Pattinson and director Denis Villeneuve, this new Bond entry needs to be populated with the very best supporting players Jeff Bezos’s money can buy.

With that in mind, here’s our dream casting for the seven most important non-Bond roles in the new film.

The Bond franchise has been around for decades, and the films are often a reflection of both the world around them and the current state of moviemaking. The Timothy Dalton era was gritty and grounded as the Cold War wound down; the Daniel Craig movies were serialized in the age of cinematic universes. For a modern-day Bond, then, we should have a villain that feels made for the 2020s. In other words: cast a sinister nerd—and more specifically, cast Samuel Blenkin.

In biopics and documentaries alike, tech bros are cinema’s latest villain du jour. Between the untold economic and environmental damage they've caused in the real world, nobody is going to feel bad about these guys being painted in an unflattering light. In that respect, Blenkin would be a fun casting. If Tenet was a great test run for Pattinson as 007, then Alien: Earth, in which Blenkin plays an impetuous tech bro with the gall to mess around with Xenomorphs (!!!), is proof that he could bring the same (respectfully) punchable energy to Bond. Say what you will about Zack Snyder’s DC movies, but picking the actor who played Mark Zuckerberg to be his Lex Luthor was ahead of the curve. Bond would be wise to meet the moment.

Runner-up: Jensen Huang (with the leather jacket, obviously).

The next M has big shoes to fill. Dame Judi Dench played the character across eight films and two separate Bonds over a period of 20 years, and Ralph Fiennes then made the role his own (as he always does), taking over the mantle for Daniel Craig’s final three films.

But sometimes, the obvious pick is the right one. Emma Thompson is acting royalty with a commanding air of authority, which is exactly what M calls for. I can just as easily picture her chastising Bond for a reckless bit of espionage as I can see her delivering some characteristically bone-dry British wit. Imagine how fucking electric a Pattinson-Thompson tête-à-tête would be.

Runner-up: Kristin Scott Thomas or Fiona Shaw.

We haven’t had an American Bond Girl since Halle Berry in Die Another Day, a film that, unfortunately, doesn’t hold up on rewatch on account of [gestures at Pierce Brosnan surfing a CGI tsunami]. Let’s have Bond dip back stateside with one of Hollywood’s most exciting young stars—and one whose name already sounds like that of a Bond Girl—in Chase Infiniti. Her resume is small but impressive: the emotional center of Paul Thomas Anderson’s Best Picture-winning One Battle After Another, a supporting role in Apple TV’s Presumed Innocent, and the lead of the Handmaid’s Tale spinoff The Testaments. And if Infiniti’s on-screen work isn’t enough to move the needle, she’s rocked enough red carpet looks to prove she knows how to make an eye-popping entrance. For a Bond Girl, that’s half the battle.

Runner-up: Margaret Qualley, mostly because she basically auditioned to be a Bond Girl at the 97th Academy Awards’ Bond tribute.

Aimee Lou Wood’s vibe as a performer is, in a word, cute. In her most notable performances—The White Lotus and Sex Education chief among them—there’s a natural warmth and mischievousness that would make her a fun scene partner for Pattinson’s Bond. Moneypenny is traditionally the one person at MI6 who can get flirty with Bond without worrying about getting a lecture from M after the fact. Wood has the charm and comic timing to make that dynamic sing.

Runner-up if Moneypenny becomes Irish: Nicola Coughlan.

Pattinson, Anne Hathaway, and (quite deservedly) Samantha Morton have been receiving much of the praise for their work in The Odyssey, but Himesh Patel’s beleaguered Eurylochus might be the film’s unsung hero. Now, he can pivot to playing the Bond franchise’s underappreciated MVP in Q: a perpetually put-upon tech genius who has to watch a reckless womanizer repeatedly destroy million-dollar prototypes. Patel has the dry, exasperated delivery down pat, and he’d be a perfect straight man for Pattinson’s particular brand of chaos (and it would mark a more-than-welcome Tenet reunion). Perhaps Q will belatedly give Patel the accolades he deserved for The Odyssey. (Also known as the Rhea Seehorn Principle.)

Runner-up: Matt Berry in character as Laszlo Cravensworth.

This might be recency bias, because I just watched Kelvin Harrison Jr. in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (say that three times fast). Harrison Jr. is Beetee Latier in the prequel, who was previously played by none other than … Jeffrey Wright. Credit where it’s due: Harrison Jr. does a mean Jeffrey Wright impression in the film.

However, we don’t need to see Harrison Jr. reheat his Wright impression in the new Bond. What I’ve admired in everything I’ve seen him in is how chameleonic he can be—to the extent that you could conceivably cast him in just about any role and he’d find a way to make it his own. (There’s no better evidence that he could play a killer spy than his performance in the psychological thriller Luce, where his character is eerily hard to get a read on.) I want a fresh take on Leiter, and the one thing we can say for Harrison Jr.: he’ll deliver on that promise.

Runner-up: John David Washington for peak Tenet vibes.

Look, I get it: Do we really need Tormund Giantsbane 2.0 in a Bond movie? But Hivju doesn’t deserve to be defined by that role for the rest of his career. He’s got the kind of outsized screen presence that demands an at-bat as a Bond henchman. (You can totally picture him getting excited by Bond drawing blood during a fight.) Sure, Villeneuve isn’t exactly known for humor in his projects, but Bond films have a long tradition of colorful henchmen, and Hivju could dial up the menace without taking himself too seriously. Give him a gimmick, a tweed suit, and no more than four lines of dialogue, and I promise that Hivju will steal every scene he’s in.

Runner-up: Olivier Richters for that Reacher season 3 fight scene alone.

Miles Surrey is a Brooklyn-based culture writer who covers television, film, and whatever your dad is interested in. His work can also be found at The Ringer, Vox, Vice, and The A.V. Club.

#4843. Tether invokes The Big Short in swipe at S&P over USDT reserve risks

S&P Global made no downward adjustment in its latest Stablecoin Stability Assessment, as 5 is the lowest available score.

S&P Global Ratings has kept Tether’s USDt at the lowest level on its stablecoin stability scale as riskier assets take up a growing share of the token’s reserves.

In a report published Nov. 18, S&P scored USDt’s ability to hold its dollar peg at 5 (weak). The assessment is unchanged from November 2025.

Higher-risk holdings, including gold, Bitcoin (BTC), public equities, secured loans and corporate bonds, were equivalent to 28% of USDt (USDT) in circulation as of Sept. 30, up from 24% a year earlier. “A significant drop in the value of these assets could lead to USDT being undercollateralized,” S&P said in the report.

“The problem is S&P’s framework, not our reserves,” Tether told Cointelegraph. “Their own history shows the underlying problem,” it added, referencing The Big Short, the film about the 2008 financial crisis.

Tether’s Sept. 30 reserve report, attested by BDO, showed approximately $191.5 billion in assets against $183.5 billion in liabilities, leaving roughly $7.95 billion in excess assets. The agency added that it found further weaknesses but made no downward adjustment “because our assessment cannot be lower than 5.”

Among the additional weaknesses highlighted by S&P was the regulatory oversight of El Salvador, where Tether relocated in January 2025.

According to the report, the National Commission of Digital Assets of El Salvador (CNAD), the regulatory body which oversees Tether in the country, requires 70% of the reserves to be held in assets that can be liquidated within 30 days. The company said they considered the framework “broad,” allowing for the inclusion of relatively high-risk assets like gold, BTC and loans.

The S&P also pointed to the lack of a requirement to segregate the reserve assets, unlike those expected by regulators in the US and Europe. As there is no publicly available information about segregation, the report states, there is no insight into how they are insulated from broader corporate risks.

USDT’s breakdown of reserve assets. Source S&P Global

In August 2026, KPMG confirmed they had issued an unqualified opinion on Tether’s 2025 accounts, in the company’s first “full independent audit”. The issuer highlighted that the audit supported the financial statements issued by the company.

However, S&P said the audited statements and the auditor’s report have not been published, which limits its ability to check the underlying information. Reserve reports also do not name the custodians and counterparties holding Tether’s assets, S&P said, and attestations remain quarterly while other stablecoins generally report monthly.

Related: Tether backs Bolivian fintech bringing USDT payments to food delivery and banking

At the time of S&P’s initial downgrade in 2025, Tether disputed the result. CEO Paolo Ardoino wrote on X, “we wear your loathing with pride,” pointing to past financial collapses as “proof” that traditional systems are broken.

Although the stability rating remained at 5, S&P ended the Nov. 18 report noting that Tether had maintained a good history of price stability, particularly in the last 12 months.

#4842. Shirley MacLaine at Home: 10 Photos of the Golden Age Great’s Life Behind the Scenes

“A house is really a life…one you’ve had or one you want to have. A new dream.” So wrote Shirley MacLaine on the first page of her memoir Sage-ing While Age-ing. And she should know. The dancer-actor-author has lived everywhere from the family home at 930 North Liberty Street in Richmond, Virginia, which she shared with her parents and younger brother (none other than Warren Beatty) to Manhattan apartments, Malibu beach cottages, and New Mexican desert ranches. And that’s just in this lifetime; MacLaine believes she has come around again through several incarnations, even writing books about her experience as a nongendered being in the Lemurian era, and another go-round on the lost continent of Atlantis.

In the 10 images below, we focus on MacLaine’s current incarnation, stepping into the Oscar-winner’s homes to see the star of Steel Magnolias and Downton Abbey at work, at play, and dancing on air.

MacLaine relaxes with a magazine in 1954.

At 20, MacLaine was a chorus girl on Broadway and the understudy for Carol Haney in The Pajama Game. When Haney twisted her ankle, MacLaine (who had changed her last name from Beaty to an alternate spelling of her mother’s maiden name, MacLean), replaced her for two weeks. Alfred Hitchcock spotted her and cast her in The Trouble with Harry, and Hal Walis signed her to a five-year studio contract, which led her to move to California. This 1954 shot shows her reading a magazine at home in Malibu, where she rented a tiny beachfront apartment. “Each home was a palace and a new jolt. They loomed on cultivated hilltops or nestled in L-shapes and U-shapes on shaded slopes, jewel-like habitations set in acres of jade carpet,” MacLaine recalled in her memoir Don’t Fall Off the Mountain. “We stared at the fairyland until our eyes hurt and our sense of reality reminded us that we were flat broke.”

When MacLaine moved from New York to California, she writes in Don’t Fall Off the Mountain, “sunshine bled from every corner and the dazzling white buildings gave me a permanent squint.” The happy gaze is on full display here in on the beach in front of the Malibu one-bedroom she and husband Steve Parker rented, which was not white, but a weathered wood cottage on stilts.

MacLaine and Parker, making the most of their outdoor shower in 1955.

“When I met Steve Parker, the attraction was immediate,” MacLaine writes in her photo-driven memoir The Wall of Life. She first encountered the businessman in New York, where, before he proposed, he informed her he was “undercover with military intelligence and work in Japan regularly, as well as other places throughout the world.” Here, Parker sneaks up on MacLaine in the one-bedroom, one-bathroom Malibu pad’s bonus outdoor shower.

The newlyweds on their home’s deck in Malibu in March, 1955.

This 1955 shot captures a rare moment of togetherness for MacLaine and Parker at their Malibu beach house. He often lived in Japan while she made films. “I’m not sure I would say that Steve and I had a happy marriage, but it was a satisfied one,” MacLaine wrote in The Wall of Life. “He had a mistress in Japan and I had whoever I was with.” But in their SoCal haven, they experienced their first taste of married life. “I was up every morning at four-thirty trying to be a housewife—ironing cleaning, and experimenting with the cookbook,” MacLaine wrote in Don’t Fall Off the Mountain. “At six Steve drove me to the studio, where we shot the final sequences of The Trouble with Harry.”

MacLaine dancing on the beach in front of her home in Malibu.

MacLaine, shown here leaping on the beach in front of her home, trained as a dancer since age three. “As I recall my life, I have come to understand that the physicality of dance was the most influential force,” she wrote in The Wall of Life. Here, MacLaine shows of her skills at the rental property she described in Don’t Fall Off the Mountain as “a tiny, one-bedroom apartment in a building set high on pilings that shook with each wave that crashed beneath it.”

This 1955 publicity shot shows MacLaine studying a script under Parker’s adoring eye in their Malibu home. While the residence’s knotty pine walls were peak mid-’50s rec room decor, MacLaine recalls Hollywood looking down on her living arrangements as her star was on the rise. She imagines the whisperings about her in Don’t Fall Off the Mountain: “She’s STILL living in a one-room shack at the beach. She’s STILL married to that man, what’s his name?”

MacLaine plays with her dog at home in 1956.

In this March 1956 photo, MacLaine plays with her boxer at home in Malibu. Six months later, on September 1, her daughter Sachi Parker would be born, inspiring MacLaine to move her new family to larger digs “in the Malibu colony with a spare room for Sachi’s new nurse-caretaker,” she wrote in The Wall of Life. “Our first year together felt like we were beach camping. I never wondered if the lifestyle was good for her, and she was never sick.” In 1963, architect Cliff Mays built an eight-unit Malibu apartment building where MacLaine would claim the top floor, which boasted six bedrooms, four baths, and a deck overlooking the ocean. She retained the property for 30 years until relocating to New Mexico, telling The Los Angeles Times, “I feel the high desert calling me.”

Shirley MacLaine in full 1970s style: maxidress, long hair. and aggressive shag carpet.

In 1972, MacLaine was spending most of her time in an apartment at 400 East 52nd Street after filming her short-lived TV series Shirley’s World. The building is part of the Southgate complex, which opened in 1931, but MacLaine did not adhere to the edifice’s Art Deco style—note the thick shag carpeting and the East Asian–inspired art on the walls. Dancer Tommy Tune bought the penthouse of the building after visiting MacLaine in her apartment.

Describing her life in New York in the 1970s, MacLaine wrote in You Can Get There from Here that “on any given day, I would mosey into Serendipity for a frozen mocha, plunder the skirt shop at Bloomingdale’s, walk to the Village and back until I reached Beekman Place at sunset and breathed in the smell of the East River.… I wanted to sit in my apartment for hours, watching all the news shows, and eating cinnamon buns from the automat.”

In this 1980 photo of MacLaine at the Southgate, her hair is different but the floral sofa remains as it was in 1972. In the years between 1972 and 1980, “I did just three films. I don’t think I got any good scripts in that period, but I didn’t care and was honestly more interested in seeing the world and understanding what was going on in it.” She made a documentary in China, campaigned for George McGovern and Jimmy Carter, and did live shows in New York and London. She was drawn back to Hollywood to make The Turning Point, and won an Oscar for her work in 1983’s Terms of Endearment.

Today, MacLaine’s New Mexico ranch is on the market, and, at age 92, she has been spotted out and about in her old stomping grounds: Malibu.
